translation_en:
Sun Zhenzong, registered in a civilian household in Jinjiang County, Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian, was a National University student specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Desheng; he ranked first in birth order, was aged thirty-eight, and was born on the second day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Chonggao, his grandfather Fu, and his father Rong; his mother was née Yang. His father was living and his mother deceased. His elder brothers were Jing, Qian, and Hou, and his younger brothers Yangzong, Zhuanzong, Huizong, and Tingzong. He married a woman née Yang. He placed seventy-second in the Fujian Provincial Examination and two hundred twenty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Yangda, registered in an official household of Suiyang Guard, Henan, was a student of the Suizhou government school specializing in the Book of Rites. His courtesy name was Zili; he ranked second in birth order, was aged thirty, and was born on the seventh day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Rong, his grandfather Tong, and his father Han, an Instructor; his mother was née Wu. Both parents were living. His elder brother Yangxiang was a Secretary in the Ministry of War, and his younger brothers were Yanglian, Yangmeng, Yangwu, and Yangtian. He married a woman née Guo and subsequently a woman née Wei. He placed seventeenth in the Henan Provincial Examination and two hundred thirty-second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhao Tijing, registered in a military household in Taigu County, Taiyuan Prefecture, Shanxi, was a National University student specializing in the Book of Poetry. His courtesy name was Keli; he ranked first in birth order, was aged thirty-two, and was born on the twenty-third day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jima, his grandfather Zhongfang, and his father Qing; his mother was née Duan. Both parents were deceased. His younger brothers were Tigong and Tishu. He married a woman née Wu. He placed fifty-second in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and two hundred seventy-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Peng Fan, registered in a civilian household in Hanzhou, Chengdu Prefecture, Sichuan, was a National University student specializing in the Book of Poetry. His courtesy name was Shihong; he ranked third in birth order, was aged thirty-two, and was born on the seventeenth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Fuming, his grandfather Xun, and his father Zhongjia; his mother was née Yang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Lu and his younger brother Zhe. He married a woman née He. He placed twenty-fourth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and one hundred forty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wu Zidong 吳自峒, courtesy name Bogao, was registered in Tongcheng County, Anqing Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, in a civilian household. An additional student of the county Confucian school, he specialized in the Book of Documents. He ranked fifth in family order and was twenty-seven years old, born on the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Zhishan; his grandfather, Zuo, was posthumously awarded the title of Bureau Director in the Ministry of War; his father, Xi, was a Right Administration Vice Commissioner; and his mother, née Lu, was granted the title Lady of Suitability. His mother alone survived. His elder brothers were Ziyue, Zixian, Ziheng, Zilong, and Zinan, and his younger brother was Zixin. He married a woman née Fang. He placed 107th in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 254th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Fu Wenzao 傅文藻, courtesy name Zongli, was registered in Yin County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household. A student of the Imperial University, he specialized in the Book of Changes. He ranked twenty-fourth in family order and was thirty-six years old, born on the eighteenth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Yu; his grandfather, Zhen, held a seventh-rank prestige title; his father, Xiang, was a Subprefectural Judge; and his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother, Wenpu, was a County Registrar, and his younger brothers were Wenpei, Wentai, and Wenzhan. He married a woman née Qiu. He placed seventy-fifth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and forty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ren Ruliang 任汝亮, courtesy name Boyin, was registered in Yishi County, Puzhou Subprefecture, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, in a military household. A student of the Imperial University, he specialized in the Book of Songs. He ranked first in family order and was thirty-two years old, born on the twentieth day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Yi; his grandfather was Hong; his father, Que, was an Assistant Prefect; and his mother was née Wang. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Ruwei, and his younger brothers were Rushi, Rugong, and Ruyu. He married a woman née Jing and subsequently married another woman née Jing. He placed third in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 118th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zheng Lüchun 鄭履淳, courtesy name Shuchu, was registered in Xiushui County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a civilian household, and was a native of Haiyan County. A student of the Imperial University, he specialized in the Book of Documents. He ranked first in family order and was twenty-seven years old, born on the twenty-second day of the third month. His great-grandfather, Yan, was Vice Superintendent of Maritime Trade and was successively awarded the posthumous titles Grand Master for Aid in Governance and Minister of Justice. His grandfather, Rutai, was an Assistant Instructor, received the honorary title Secretary, and was successively awarded the posthumous titles Grand Master for Aid in Governance and Minister of Justice. His father, Xiao, was Minister of Justice. His mother and stepmother were both née Liu and were both posthumously awarded the title Lady; his birth mother was née Shen. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Ji, Fa, Cong, Zhu, Di 滴, and Di 滌; his younger brothers were Lüzhun, a student of the Imperial University, Lüshun, and Xun. He married a woman née Zhu. He placed 128th in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and fifty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Li Shikong, registered in Kaizhou, Daming Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a civilian household and was an attached student of the department school. He specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Zixiao; he ranked first among his brothers and was thirty-eight years old, born on the nineteenth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Rang, his grandfather Biao, and his father Jue; his mother was née Zhao. His father was living and his mother deceased. His wife was née Zhang. He placed seventy-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 264th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Mu Wenxi, registered in Dongming County, Daming Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, belonged to a military household and was a county school student. He specialized in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Jingfu; he ranked first among his brothers and was thirty years old, born on the eleventh day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shan, his grandfather Jin, and his father Chen Shi [?]; his mother was née Tao. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Nan, and his wife was née Zhang. He placed eighty-fourth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 262nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhou Yijing, registered in Shangrao County, Guangxin Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a civilian household and was a student of the Imperial University. He specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Yonghan; he ranked fifteenth among his brothers and was thirty-six years old, born on the fifteenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Junzhang, his grandfather Ji, and his father Li; his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Yicheng. His wife was née Tan, and his subsequent wife was née Mao. He placed forty-fifth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and fifty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Wensui, registered in Linchuan County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a civilian household and was an added-quota student of the county school. He specialized in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Ruxiang; he ranked ninth among his brothers and was twenty-eight years old, born on the twenty-first day of the sixth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xuchu, his grandfather Ji, and his father Xing; his mother was née Liu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Chi; his younger brothers were Wenhuang, Wenhuan〔a tribute scholar (gongshi)〕, Wenyu, and Wenzhao. His wife was née Shuai. He placed second in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and eleventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wei Ruyi was registered in a military household in Jingyang County, Xi’an Prefecture, Shaanxi. A student of the Imperial University, he specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Zixing; he ranked sixth in family order and was thirty-nine years old, born on the nineteenth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Xiang; his grandfather, Zan, and father, Hongren, were both county magistrates. His mother was née Guo. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Rufu, Rubi, Ruxiang, Rucheng, and Ruzuo; his younger brothers were Rucheng, Ruji, Ruzhou, Rumei, Rune, Rugui, and Ruxiang. He married a woman née Tian. He placed fifty-first in the Shaanxi Provincial Examination and 258th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Nian was registered in a civilian household in Yangxin County, Wuding Subprefecture, Jinan Prefecture, Shandong, and was originally from Dingyuan County, Fengyang Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A student of the Imperial University, he specialized in the Record of Rites. His courtesy name was Zishi; he ranked first in family order and was thirty-nine years old, born on the thirtieth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather was Xian. His grandfather, Zuo, held an honorary rank for longevity and was posthumously granted the title of bureau director in the Ministry of Revenue. His father, Li, was a bureau director in that ministry. His father’s former wife, née Zong, was posthumously granted the title Lady of Suitability; his mother, née Zhang, was granted the same title. His father was deceased, and he attended upon his surviving mother. His elder brothers were Fan, Shi, Ren, and Zai; his younger brothers were Zhen, Gu, Ni, Yue, and Fu. He married a woman née Ding. He placed seventy-fourth in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 297th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Shanyan was registered in a civilian household in Cheng’an County, Guangping Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A student of the county school, he specialized in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Ziyuan; he ranked first in family order and was twenty-six years old, born on the eighteenth day of the eighth month. His great-grandfather was Yun, his grandfather Ming, and his father Yuan; his mother was née Shi. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Dao, Tian, Le, and Qin. He married a woman née Shi. He placed fifty-seventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 103rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

He Wenwei was registered in an official household of Dingliao Rear Guard, Liaodong, and was originally from Yugan County, Raozhou Prefecture, Jiangxi. A student of the school of the Liaodong Regional Military Commission, he specialized in the Classic of Documents. His courtesy name was Weizheng; he ranked fifth in family order and was twenty-nine years old, born on the second day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Neng. His grandfather, Cong, held an honorary title for public benefaction and was posthumously granted the title of subprefect. His father, Tang, was a prefectural vice prefect. His father’s former wife, née Miao, was posthumously granted the title Lady of Suitability; his mother, née Sun, was granted the same title. His stepmother was née Liang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Lun, Wenshou, Wenyin, Wenshao (a garrison official at Fuzhen [?]), Wenqi, and Wenchun; his younger brother was Wencai. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed ninety-eighth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 180th in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
皇帝制曰朕惟自昔
帝王莫聖於堯舜
史稱堯舜垂衣裳
而天下治矣然當
其時下民猶咨洚
===
水為灾有苗弗率
則猶有未盡治平
者豈二帝固弗之
恤歟抑其臣任之
於下而上可以無

translation_en: The Emperor's decree reads: “I consider that, among emperors and kings since antiquity, none surpassed Yao and Shun in sagehood. The histories state that Yao and Shun let their robes hang down, and all under Heaven was well governed. Yet in their time the common people still lamented, floods brought disaster, and the Miao would not submit. Thus there were still respects in which order and peace had not been fully achieved. Could it be that the two sovereigns simply paid these matters no heed? Or was it that their ministers took responsibility below, while the sovereign above could take no …

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
為不然何以垂衣
而治也三代莫盛
於成周宣王中興
詩稱召伯平淮夷
方叔征蠻荆吉甫
伐玁狁惟得其人
以分命之是以不
勞而治朕常嘉之
甚慕之朕撫天下
四十有一年于此

punctuated: 為？不然，何以垂衣而治也？三代莫盛於成周，宣王中興，詩稱召伯平淮夷，方叔征蠻荆，吉甫伐玁狁，惟得其人以分命之，是以不勞而治。朕常嘉之，甚慕之。朕撫天下四十有一年于此
translation_en: …remain without acting? If not, how could they have governed merely by letting their robes hang down? Among the Three Dynasties, none flourished more than Zhou. During King Xuan’s restoration, the Book of Odes praised the Earl of Shao for pacifying the Huaiyi, Fang Shu for campaigning against the Man of Jing, and Ji Fu for attacking the Xianyun. It was only because the right men were found and assigned their respective commands that order was achieved without toil. I have always commended this and greatly admired it. I have now governed All under Heaven for forty-one years…

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:

祖宗選任文武大吏

害而遂其生兢業
===

者水旱為灾黎民
阻饑戎狄時警邊
圉弗靖而南賊尤
甚歷時越歲尚未

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
底寧豈有司莫體
朕心皆殘民以逞
有以致之歟抑選
任者未得其人或
多失職歟將疆圉
===
之臣未能殫力制
禦玩寇者歟夫朕
有愛民之心而澤
未究有遏亂之志
而効未臻固以今

We have the desire to cherish the people, yet Our beneficence has not reached them fully; We have the resolve to suppress disorder, yet results have not been attained. Surely this is because today…

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
昔不類未得如古
任事之臣耳茲欲
使上下協慮政事
具修兵足而寇患
以除民安而邦本
===
以固灾咎可弭困
窮可復以媲美虞
周之治其何道而
可爾諸士悉心陳
列勿憚勿隱朕將

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
臣徐時行
臣對臣聞帝王之御極也體君道以奉天心
而後可以建久安長治之業肅臣紀以奉天
職而後可以成內修外攘之功何則人君者
天之所授以統一萬方而臨馭兆民者也其
位尊其任重故君道常主乎逸人臣者天之
所命以左右一人而分理庶政者也其分卑
其事蹟故臣道常主乎勞君能奉天以端拱
於上而以其事責諸臣則無爲而化成不言
而功著若於穆之運玄機之宰不假於推遷
===
之力而自然造物者矣是謂能奉天心而久
安長治之業可建也臣能奉君以奔走於下
而以其身致之君則同心以共濟協忠以體
國若四時之佐五行之吏各效其宣布之能
而罔有違天者矣是謂能奉天職而內修外
攘之功可成也不然則一人之身萬幾攸萃
安能一一而理之而庶官之衆各有司存能
不蹈於瘝曠之咎哉故君必率臣以圖久安
長治之業臣必輔君以樹內修外攘之功則
□氣溢而宇宙清寧理道昌而民物康乂順

Your servant, Xu Shixing.

Your servant replies: I have heard that when emperors and kings ascend the supreme throne, only by embodying the Way of the ruler to serve Heaven’s intentions can they establish enduring peace and lasting order; only by enforcing discipline among their ministers to fulfill the duties entrusted by Heaven can they accomplish internal reform and the repulsion of external threats. Why is this? The ruler is one whom Heaven has invested with authority to unite the myriad regions and govern the countless people. His position is exalted and his responsibility weighty; hence the Way of the ruler principally consists in repose. Ministers are those whom Heaven has appointed to assist the One Man and share the administration of the many affairs of government. Their station is subordinate and their tasks demanding [?]; hence the Way of the minister principally consists in exertion. If the ruler can serve Heaven by sitting upright with hands folded above and holding his ministers responsible for affairs, transformation will be achieved without his taking action, and accomplishments will become manifest without his speaking. He will resemble the workings of profound Heaven and the governance of its mysterious mechanism, which naturally create all things without relying on the force of deliberate propulsion. This is what is meant by serving Heaven’s intentions, whereby enduring peace and lasting order can be established.

If ministers can serve their ruler by hastening about their duties below and devoting themselves wholly to him, they will work with one mind toward common success and unite in loyalty to care for the state. Like the assistants of the four seasons and the officers of the Five Phases, each will exercise his capacity to carry Heaven’s operations into effect, and none will act contrary to Heaven. This is what is meant by fulfilling the duties entrusted by Heaven, whereby internal reform and the repulsion of external threats can be accomplished. Otherwise, with the myriad affairs of state converging upon the person of the One Man, how could he manage them individually? And could the multitude of officials, each with his assigned responsibilities, avoid the blame of neglecting their offices? Thus the ruler must lead his ministers in seeking enduring peace and lasting order, and ministers must assist their ruler in accomplishing internal reform and the repulsion of external threats. …are worthy, and all affairs prosper!” This means that when an enlightened ruler presides above and worthy ministers assist him, all affairs can be properly ordered. It also says: “Heaven hears and sees clearly; the sage takes this as his model, and ministers reverently follow.” This means that when the ruler can model himself on Heaven, those serving as ministers naturally follow him with reverence, none daring to act contrary to him. Thus the ruler, as the head, models himself on Heaven above. Taking Heaven as his model in hearing, he occupies a lofty position yet hears those below, and can hear all under Heaven while seated, without exertion. Taking Heaven as his model in seeing, he shines brilliantly upon those below, and can illuminate the four quarters while seated, without exertion. The ruler thus follows the Way of Heaven through nonaction. Ministers, as the limbs, reverently follow below. Exercising the ruler’s hearing on his behalf, they ensure that information about everything beneficial or harmful under Heaven reaches him without obstruction. Exercising his sight on his behalf, they thoroughly discern the people’s joys and sorrows, overlooking nothing. Ministers thus undertake active duties in fulfillment of the offices entrusted by Heaven.

Hence, in the age of Tang and Yu, the myriad states were brought into harmony, the four quarters were stirred as by the wind, and a flourishing age of cultured enlightenment arose. Yao and Shun, rulers whose powers of hearing and seeing attained the utmost sagacity, silently conducted government through nonaction. They also had such ministers as Yu, Gao, Ji, Xie, and Boyi, who together assisted in establishing great peace. When the common people lamented, when floods brought disaster, and when the Youmiao refused obedience, it was not that Yao and Shun were unconcerned. Rather, their loyal and worthy assistants were fully capable of furthering their imperial plans, and their upright, corrective advisers could extend the imperial Way. To relieve those suffering hardship and hunger, there were ministers who nurtured all the people; to rescue those engulfed by the floods, there were ministers capable of tireless labor; to bring to submission those who relied upon their strongholds, there were ministers who helped advance the ruler’s virtue. These ministers served their ruler as they served Heaven. Diligently united in reverence and common respect, none dared indulge in idleness or leisure. 曰唐虞此堯舜得臣之明驗也周宣之世海
內乂安矣國勢寢隆矣文武之業復矣宣王
以聰明有道之君嗣守無疆之業而又有召
虎方叔吉甫之臣夾輔中興之治故淮夷之
猖亂也荆蠻之不靖也玁狁之虔劉也宣王
非不之慮也惟其位元宰者才兼乎文武總
元戎者勳聯乎將相有宣威江漢之臣而淮
夷率俾有壯猷南國之臣而荆蠻來威有薄
伐太原之臣而玁狁于襄諸臣者其事君亦
===
如事天也惴惴焉矢心協力罔敢戲豫也故
宣王有繼述之思而終以成再造之績至今
稱中興之盛者必曰成周此宣王得臣之明
驗也堯舜宣王之為君法天道以無為而唐
虞成周之臣奉天職以有事則所以建久安

終得以享垂衣之治。至今稱中天之盛者，必曰唐虞，此堯舜得臣之明驗也。周宣之世，海內乂安矣，國勢寢隆矣，文武之業復矣。宣王以聰明有道之君，嗣守無疆之業，而又有召虎、方叔、吉甫之臣，夾輔中興之治。故淮夷之猖亂也，荆蠻之不靖也，玁狁之虔劉也，宣王非不之慮也。惟其位元宰者，才兼乎文武；總元戎者，勳聯乎將相。有宣威江漢之臣，而淮夷率俾；有壯猷南國之臣，而荆蠻來威；有薄伐太原之臣，而玁狁于襄。諸臣者，其事君亦如事天也，惴惴焉矢心協力，罔敢戲豫也。故宣王有繼述之思，而終以成再造之績。至今稱中興之盛者，必曰成周，此宣王得臣之明驗也。堯舜宣王之為君，法天道以無為，而唐虞成周之臣，奉天職以有事，則所以建久安長治之業，成內修外攘之功者，豈偶然哉？
臣伏覩陛下臨御以來，四十有一年矣。上帝之申眷，不為不隆，而誠敬愈篤；祖宗之成業，不為不固，而仁孝愈純。
translation_en:
…in the end they were able to enjoy government conducted with robes hanging down, without active intervention. To this day, those who speak of prosperity at its zenith invariably cite Tang and Yu, the ages of Yao and Shun. This is clear proof that Yao and Shun obtained worthy ministers. In the age of King Xuan of Zhou, all within the seas was orderly and peaceful, the power of the state steadily increased, and the achievement of Kings Wen and Wu was restored. An intelligent and principled ruler, King Xuan inherited and preserved an enduring royal enterprise; he also had ministers such as Shao Hu, Fang Shu, and Jifu to assist him in restoring good government. Thus, when the Huai Yi rebelled, the Jing Man were unsettled, and the Xianyun wrought slaughter, it was not that King Xuan felt no concern. Rather, those occupying the position of chief minister possessed both civil and military talents, while those commanding the great armies combined the achievements of generals and chief councillors. There were ministers who displayed his might along the Jiang and Han rivers, and the Huai Yi obeyed; ministers who devised mighty plans for the southern lands, and the Jing Man submitted in awe; ministers who marched against the enemy at Taiyuan, and the Xianyun were driven away. These ministers, too, served their ruler as they served Heaven. With trembling vigilance, they pledged their hearts and joined their efforts, never daring to indulge in frivolity or ease. Thus King Xuan, intent on carrying forward his predecessors’ work, ultimately accomplished the restoration of the realm. To this day, those who speak of the splendor of a dynastic resurgence invariably cite the restored Zhou. This is clear proof that King Xuan obtained worthy ministers. As rulers, Yao, Shun, and King Xuan modeled themselves on the Way of Heaven through nonaction, while the ministers of Tang, Yu, and Zhou discharged Heaven’s duties through active service. Could their establishment of lasting peace and enduring order, and their accomplishments in strengthening government internally and repelling threats externally, have been mere chance?
Your servant humbly observes that forty-one years have passed since Your Majesty ascended the throne. The renewed favor of the Lord on High has certainly been abundant, yet your sincerity and reverence grow ever deeper; the foundations laid by your imperial ancestors have certainly been secure, yet your benevolence and filial devotion grow ever purer…

You have composed a record on revering Heaven to express your sincere devotion to serving it, and a poem on ancestral virtue to voice your resolve to follow your forebears. Your concern is deeply engaged with the people's suffering, and you assign officials specific responsibilities. Within the realm, you hold prefects and magistrates accountable for results, yet year after year you continue to dispatch officials to inspect and supervise them. On the frontiers, you entrust affairs to generals, yet invariably confer greater authority upon those appointed supreme commanders. Not a single thought of yours is apart from the people's suffering; not a single utterance fails to show concern for the troubles of the state. Your servant can thus perceive, with reverence, that Your Majesty's heart is the very heart of Yao and Shun, beyond even King Xuan of Zhou's ability to match. Now auspicious signs gather and all four numinous creatures appear: these surely suffice to manifest Your Majesty's lofty virtue and magnificent achievements, surpassing those of a hundred generations. Yet when excessive rains bring disaster, the fields suffer inundation; when severe drought wreaks havoc, the farmlands face withering and desiccation. Japanese raiders make sudden incursions in the southeast, leaving the seas unsettled; vile barbarians run rampant in the northwest, repeatedly alarming the frontier. Worse still, the position of Liao and Ji grows daily more isolated and precarious, while the bandits of Jiangyou spread farther with each passing year. These are utterly unfitting conditions for a sage's age. This is precisely a time for concern for the people such as Yao and Shun showed, a day for strenuous effort such as King Xuan of Zhou displayed.
Your servant has reverently read the imperial composition, which says: “Recently floods and droughts have brought disaster, and the common people have suffered hunger. The Rong and Di repeatedly cause alarms, and the frontiers are unsettled; the bandits in the south are especially troublesome. Through successive seasons and years, peace has still not been attained. Can it be that the responsible officials fail to understand Our heart and all injure the people to gratify themselves, thereby bringing this about?” That Your Majesty should speak of these matters is a blessing for all lands and all their people. title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
陛下之寵榮乎凡擁旄杖鉞制閫握兵者孰非
陛下之威靈乎謂宜夙夜匪懈寢處不遑布寧謐
之化於域中揚振肅之威於閫外不負
天子而勿為聖世之瘝官也然各私其身者罔致
恤於民依各利其家者莫究心於國事内而
守令藩臬固必有旬宣惠和憂勤撫字之臣
矣然而肥己瘠民營私蠹國以催科聚斂為
能以簿書期會為急者亦多有之也外而營
屯督府固必有敵愾鷹揚嚴明果毅之臣矣
然而坐失機宜輕損威重隱敗衂以為捷幸
===
安靜以為福者亦恒有之也人臣咸若是則
何以成内脩外攘之功而佐久安長治之業
哉蓋
陛下愛民之心容保如天地而諸臣不能承宣
德意以弘康國之猷
陛下遏亂之志果决如雷霆而諸臣不能奉揚
威命以茂肅清之烈是自負於堯舜周宣之主
而有愧於唐虞成周之臣多矣及讀
聖制終篇有曰玆欲使上下協慮政事具修兵足
而寇患以除民安而邦本以固灾咎可弭困窮

translation_en:
…the favor and honors bestowed by Your Majesty? Of all those who bear command banners and battle-axes, exercise authority beyond the palace gates, and command troops, whose authority does not derive from Your Majesty’s awe-inspiring power? They should surely be unremitting day and night, with no leisure for sleep or repose, spreading peaceful governance within the realm and displaying stern military might beyond its gates. They should not fail the Son of Heaven or neglect their offices in this sage age. Yet those concerned only for themselves give no thought to the people’s livelihood, and those seeking profit for their own families give no attention to affairs of state. Among prefects, magistrates, provincial administration commissioners, and provincial surveillance commissioners serving within the realm, there must certainly be officials who spread benevolent and harmonious rule, diligently tending the people with anxious care. Yet there are also many who enrich themselves while impoverishing the people, pursue private interests while draining the state, regard the collection of taxes and exactions as ability, and make account books and reporting deadlines their urgent concern. Among those serving in military camps, garrisons, and regional command offices, there must certainly be officials who hate the enemy and soar like hawks, who are strict, discerning, resolute, and courageous. Yet there are also constantly those who let opportunities slip away through inaction, recklessly diminish their authority and prestige, conceal defeats as victories, and count themselves fortunate if all happens to remain quiet. If ministers all behave thus, how can they achieve good administration within and the repulsion of enemies without, and assist in establishing enduring peace and lasting order?
Your Majesty’s love for the people embraces and protects them like Heaven and Earth, yet your ministers cannot carry out and proclaim your benevolent intentions to advance plans for the well-being of the state. Your Majesty’s determination to suppress disorder is as decisive as thunder, yet your ministers cannot uphold and proclaim your august commands to achieve greater success in restoring peace. Thus they fail a ruler comparable to Yao, Shun, and King Xuan of Zhou, and fall far short of the ministers of Tang, Yu, and the perfected Zhou order. On reading the concluding portion of the imperial decree, I came to these words: “We now desire that those above and below deliberate together, that affairs of government be fully put in order, that military resources be sufficient to eliminate the scourge of bandits, that the people be secure and thereby the foundations of the state made firm, that calamities and misfortunes may be averted, and that hardship and poverty…”

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
可復以媲美虞周之治其何道而可臣愚以為
上者下之表也政事者臣之紀也足兵以除
寇將帥之責任也安民以固國守令之職業
也灾咎之有無困窮之復否皆由此出者也
為
今日計莫先於任人尤莫要於擇人夫
國家分職命官衆矣即列郡專城遐陬僻壤莫
不置吏盖未嘗不任人也臣以為任之而未
當也
國家衆賢歛才舊矣即銓司法曹明黜顯擢罔
===
有違例盖未嘗不擇人也臣以為擇之而未
精也任之未當與擇之未精而欲得人以裨
聖治是猶楩梓未充而需棟梁之用穮蔉弗
習而希稼穡之成臣知其弗能也故夫欲修
內治者在慎擇乎守令而已矣欲平外患者
在慎擇乎將帥而已矣董仲舒曰守令者民
之師帥所使承流而宣化者也守令而不得
其人雖日布蠲恤之令時厪惠鮮之思民猶
不被其澤也今也闔郡無文翁之化而漁獵
民資者接踵邑里無魯恭之風而朘剥民膏

可復，以媲美虞周之治，其何道而可？」臣愚以為，上者，下之表也；政事者，臣之紀也。足兵以除寇，將帥之責任也；安民以固國，守令之職業也。灾咎之有無，困窮之復否，皆由此出者也。為今日計，莫先於任人，尤莫要於擇人。夫國家分職命官衆矣，即列郡專城、遐陬僻壤，莫不置吏，盖未嘗不任人也。臣以為任之而未當也。國家衆賢歛才舊矣，即銓司法曹，明黜顯擢，罔有違例，盖未嘗不擇人也。臣以為擇之而未精也。任之未當與擇之未精，而欲得人以裨聖治，是猶楩梓未充而需棟梁之用，穮蔉弗習而希稼穡之成，臣知其弗能也。

故夫欲修內治者，在慎擇乎守令而已矣；欲平外患者，在慎擇乎將帥而已矣。董仲舒曰：「守令者，民之師帥，所使承流而宣化者也。」守令而不得其人，雖日布蠲恤之令，時厪惠鮮之思，民猶不被其澤也。今也，闔郡無文翁之化，而漁獵民資者接踵；邑里無魯恭之風，而朘剥民膏
translation_en:
…distress may be relieved, so as to rival the governance of Yu and Zhou: by what means can this be achieved?” In my humble opinion, those above are the example for those below, and affairs of government are the guiding discipline of ministers. Providing sufficient troops to eliminate bandits is the responsibility of generals and commanders; bringing peace to the people to secure the state is the duty of prefects and county magistrates. Whether calamities occur and whether distress is relieved all depend upon these things. In planning for the present, nothing takes precedence over appointing men, and nothing is more essential than choosing them carefully. The state has allocated duties and appointed many officials. Even throughout the prefectures and cities, and in distant corners and remote districts, officials are invariably installed. Thus it has certainly not failed to appoint men. Your servant believes, however, that its appointments have not been appropriate. The state has long gathered worthy men and recruited talent [?]. In the personnel-selection offices and judicial bureaus, dismissals and promotions are openly carried out, without departure from established regulations. Thus it has certainly not failed to select men. Your servant believes, however, that its selection has not been sufficiently discerning. To seek men capable of assisting Your Majesty’s sagely governance when appointments are inappropriate and selection insufficiently discerning is like requiring timber for pillars and beams before sufficient pian and zi trees have grown, or hoping for a successful harvest without practice in weeding and earthing up. Your servant knows this cannot succeed.

Thus, anyone wishing to improve internal administration need only exercise care in choosing prefects and county magistrates; anyone wishing to quell external troubles need only exercise care in choosing generals and commanders. Dong Zhongshu said: “Prefects and county magistrates are the people’s teachers and leaders, charged with receiving the influence from above and spreading its transforming instruction.” If the wrong men become prefects and county magistrates, even though orders for tax remission and relief are issued daily, and thought is continually given to kindness toward the needy, the people still do not receive these benefits. Today, throughout the prefectures there is none of Wen Weng’s transforming influence, while men who prey upon the people’s resources follow one another in succession; in the counties and villages there is none of Lu Gong’s exemplary conduct, while those who drain and strip away the people’s lifeblood…

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
者比肩以狼牧羊而暴政日聞以齒焚身而
敗官弗恤郡縣之民幾何不流離而攘竊也
必也精選用之法嚴舉劾之科其未任也試
以經濟之畧必求諳練民情通達治體而不
拘選用之途如唐之試理人策可也其既任
也責以久任之功必使吏安其官民狎其政
而不拘遷轉之格如漢之為吏長子孫可也
其任而獲效也優以格外之賞必旌之車服
崇之階銜以彰卓異之勲如漢之爵至關內
侯可也如是則有民有土之寄不輕數遷數
===
易之弊可免而人知淬勵以期不負乎優渥
之恩矣寧有守令失人之患哉孫武曰將者
三軍之命國之重任不可不知也將帥而不
得其人雖決策於
九重定計於千里猶未可以臨敵也今也操練之
律雖嚴而士無投石超距之勇衣糧之給如
故而將無搴旗陷陣之能論戰闘則縮頸而
股栗聞調遣則掩耳而口噤邊圉之寇幾何
不肆行而竊發也必也慎武舉之選嚴比試
之條有洞識兵機明習邊務者材可任也則

者比肩。以狼牧羊，而暴政日聞；以齒焚身，而敗官弗恤。郡縣之民，幾何不流離而攘竊也？必也精選用之法，嚴舉劾之科。其未任也，試以經濟之畧，必求諳練民情、通達治體，而不拘選用之途，如唐之試理人策可也。其既任也，責以久任之功，必使吏安其官、民狎其政，而不拘遷轉之格，如漢之為吏長子孫可也。其任而獲效也，優以格外之賞，必旌之車服，崇之階銜，以彰卓異之勲，如漢之爵至關內侯可也。如是，則有民有土之寄不輕，數遷數易之弊可免，而人知淬勵，以期不負乎優渥之恩矣。寧有守令失人之患哉？
孫武曰：「將者，三軍之命，國之重任，不可不知也。」將帥而不得其人，雖決策於九重、定計於千里，猶未可以臨敵也。今也，操練之律雖嚴，而士無投石超距之勇；衣糧之給如故，而將無搴旗陷陣之能。論戰闘，則縮頸而股栗；聞調遣，則掩耳而口噤。邊圉之寇，幾何不肆行而竊發也？必也慎武舉之選，嚴比試之條。有洞識兵機、明習邊務者，材可任也，則
translation_en:
…stand shoulder to shoulder. Wolves are set to tend sheep, and reports of oppressive government are heard daily; through their appetites they bring destruction upon themselves, yet care nothing for disgracing their offices. How can the people of the prefectures and counties avoid displacement and theft? The methods of selection and appointment must therefore be refined, and the rules governing recommendation and impeachment strictly enforced. Before appointment, candidates should be tested on their strategies for ordering the realm and aiding its people. Men thoroughly acquainted with the people's circumstances and versed in the essentials of government must be sought, without restricting the channels of recruitment. The Tang practice of testing candidates with policy questions on governing the people would serve. Once appointed, they should be held responsible for achievements attained through long tenure. Officials must be allowed to settle into their offices and the people to grow familiar with their administration, without rigid adherence to the regulations for promotion and transfer. The Han practice whereby officials remained in office long enough to raise children and grandchildren would serve. When they achieve results in office, they should receive generous rewards beyond the ordinary scale: carriages and robes should mark their distinction, and higher ranks and titles should honor their exceptional accomplishments. The Han practice of conferring titles as high as Marquis within the Passes would serve. In this way, the responsibility of governing people and territory would not be treated lightly, and the abuses of repeated transfers and replacements could be avoided. Men would know to exert and improve themselves, hoping not to prove unworthy of such generous imperial favor. How could there then be any fear of appointing unsuitable prefects and magistrates?
Sun Wu said: “The general is the life of the armies and bears a weighty responsibility for the state; this must be understood.” If unsuitable men are appointed as commanders, even decisions made in the innermost palace and plans laid for operations a thousand li away will not suffice to confront the enemy. Today, although the rules for military training are strict, the soldiers lack the prowess to hurl stones and leap great distances. Although clothing and provisions are supplied as before, the generals lack the ability to seize enemy standards and break through enemy formations. At talk of battle, they shrink back and their thighs tremble; on hearing orders for deployment, they cover their ears and keep their mouths shut. How can raiders along the frontiers fail to run rampant and launch sudden attacks? Selection through the military examinations must therefore be conducted carefully, and the rules for competitive testing strictly enforced. Where there are men who thoroughly understand military opportunities and are well versed in frontier affairs, whose abilities qualify them for employment, then…

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
不拘以騎射之習如任杜預以平吳可也有
摧鋒陷敵决勝先登者功可錄也則不繩以
文法之細如赦魏尚於雲中可也有保障一
方折衝萬里者權可假也則不牽以中制之
命如委充國於金城可也如是則真材不耻
於武弁良將不苦於約束而人得展布以自
效夫捍禦之能矣安有將帥失人之患哉有
賢守令以宣德化於域中則政治畢舉而內
有順治之休有名將帥以揚威靈於閫外則
紀律章明而外有威嚴之烈由是民生舉安
===
則邦本有磐石之固由是兵威日振則寇患
無潢池之虞和氣交蒸於海宇而灾害不興
頌聲流布於黔黎而困窮以復尚何不足以
成久安長治之業而追唐虞成周之盛哉抑
臣又聞之
朝廷者四方之極也純心者用人之樞也惟
陛下常存敬一之心以端拱於上而已敬則存其
心而不放一則純乎理而不雜深宮燕閒之
中而不忘乎知人安民之慮齋居邃密之際
而日嚴夫敬

punctuated:
不拘以騎射之習，如任杜預以平吳可也。有摧鋒陷敵、决勝先登者，功可錄也，則不繩以文法之細，如赦魏尚於雲中可也。有保障一方、折衝萬里者，權可假也，則不牽以中制之命，如委充國於金城可也。如是，則真材不耻於武弁，良將不苦於約束，而人得展布以自效夫捍禦之能矣，安有將帥失人之患哉？有賢守令以宣德化於域中，則政治畢舉，而內有順治之休；有名將帥以揚威靈於閫外，則紀律章明，而外有威嚴之烈。由是民生舉安，則邦本有磐石之固；由是兵威日振，則寇患無潢池之虞。和氣交蒸於海宇，而灾害不興；頌聲流布於黔黎，而困窮以復。尚何不足以成久安長治之業，而追唐虞成周之盛哉？
抑臣又聞之：朝廷者，四方之極也；純心者，用人之樞也。惟陛下常存敬一之心，以端拱於上而已。敬則存其心而不放，一則純乎理而不雜。深宮燕閒之中，而不忘乎知人安民之慮；齋居邃密之際，而日嚴夫敬
translation_en:
…do not restrict them by requirements of proficiency in mounted archery; appointing them as Du Yu was appointed to pacify Wu would be fitting. Those who break through enemy lines, secure victory, and lead the assault have achievements worthy of recognition: do not bind them with the minutiae of legal formalities; pardoning them as Wei Shang was pardoned at Yunzhong would be fitting. Those who safeguard a region and repel threats ten thousand li away may be entrusted with discretionary authority: do not constrain them with commands issued from the court; entrusting them with responsibility as Chongguo was entrusted at Jincheng would be fitting. Thus truly talented men would not be ashamed to hold military office, capable generals would not suffer under restrictions, and each could exercise his abilities and demonstrate his capacity for defense. How then could there be any concern that the wrong men had been chosen as commanders? With worthy prefects and magistrates spreading moral transformation throughout the realm, all affairs of government would be attended to, and orderly rule would bring blessings at home. With distinguished commanders displaying imperial might beyond the military gates, discipline would be manifest, and imposing authority would achieve results abroad. The people's livelihoods would thereby all be secured, and the foundation of the state would be as firm as a massive rock. Military strength would thereby grow daily, and there would be no fear of petty rebellion. Harmonious influences would rise together throughout the empire, and calamities would not arise; songs of praise would spread among the common people, and those in hardship would recover. What, then, would be lacking for establishing enduring peace and lasting good government, and matching the splendor of Tang and Yu and the flourishing Zhou?
Your servant has also heard this: the court is the pole toward which the four quarters turn; purity of mind is the pivot of employing men. Your Majesty need only constantly preserve a mind of reverent single-mindedness, sitting upright with folded hands on high. Reverence preserves the mind and keeps it from straying; single-mindedness keeps it pure in accordance with principle and free of admixture. In the leisure of the inner palace, do not forget the concerns of discerning men's abilities and bringing peace to the people; in the secluded stillness of your purified retreat, daily deepen your reverence…

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
天法
祖之忱則心正而朝廷百官皆一於正矣文武大
吏有不奉承而守令將帥有不奮勵者哉臣
不識忌諱干冒
天威無任戰慄隕越之至臣謹對
alt_text:

天威無任戰慄隕越之至臣謹對
punctuated: 天法祖之忱，則心正而朝廷百官皆一於正矣。文武大吏有不奉承，而守令將帥有不奮勵者哉？臣不識忌諱，干冒天威，無任戰慄隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en: …Heaven and emulating the ancestors: with this sincerity, Your Majesty’s mind will be upright, and the court’s hundred officials will all be united in uprightness. Could any high civil or military official fail to carry out Your Majesty’s will, or any prefect, magistrate, or military commander fail to exert himself? Your servant, ignorant of what must not be spoken, has dared to offend Your Majesty’s awe-inspiring authority. I am overcome with trembling and dread, as though about to fall. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
臣王錫爵
臣對臣聞帝王之御世也必文武並用而後
天下之治法以行必仁智相須而後天下之
治人以得何謂治法興天下之利除天下之
害使遠邇胥匡中外禔福而順治威嚴永孚
于休者皆法也何謂治人以天下之才任天
下之事使明良一德事使同心而奔走禦侮
各稱其職者皆人也人固緣法而舉法必待
人而行是故欲行治法則修文以布懷柔之
德經武以彰撻伐之威而安內攘外之功兼
===
舉之矣欲得治人則本仁以弘翕受之公盡
智以昭旌別之典而輔理承化之績恒賴之
矣自古太平之世君逸於上臣勞於下而四
方為之嚮風八表為之順則者恃有此具也
不然上雖有仁聖之主而下無忠良之佐君
雖有願治之志而民不得被至治之澤非惟
官失其人而法亦因之以不舉是豈可無轉
移之術哉欽惟
皇帝陛下以
聖神文武之資立仁義中正之極恭己垂裳而百

punctuated:
臣王錫爵。

臣對：臣聞帝王之御世也，必文武並用而後天下之治法以行，必仁智相須而後天下之治人以得。何謂治法？興天下之利，除天下之害，使遠邇胥匡，中外禔福，而順治威嚴永孚于休者，皆法也。何謂治人？以天下之才任天下之事，使明良一德，事使同心，而奔走禦侮，各稱其職者，皆人也。人固緣法而舉，法必待人而行。是故欲行治法，則修文以布懷柔之德，經武以彰撻伐之威，而安內攘外之功兼舉之矣。欲得治人，則本仁以弘翕受之公，盡智以昭旌別之典，而輔理承化之績恒賴之矣。自古太平之世，君逸於上，臣勞於下，而四方為之嚮風，八表為之順則者，恃有此具也。不然，上雖有仁聖之主，而下無忠良之佐；君雖有願治之志，而民不得被至治之澤。非惟官失其人，而法亦因之以不舉，是豈可無轉移之術哉？

欽惟皇帝陛下，以聖神文武之資，立仁義中正之極，恭己垂裳而百
translation_en:
Your servant Wang Xijue.

Your servant replies: I have heard that, when emperors and kings govern the world, only by employing both civil and military means can they put the methods of governing the realm into practice; only when benevolence and wisdom support one another can they obtain the men who will govern it. What are methods of government? Promoting all that benefits the realm and removing all that harms it; bringing both distant and nearby regions into proper order and securing well-being within and beyond; ensuring that orderly government and stern authority forever accord with what is good—all these belong to methods. What are men who govern? Entrusting the affairs of the realm to its talented men, so that an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers share a single virtue, those who serve and those who direct act with one mind [?], and those who hasten to their duties and resist foreign aggression each fulfill their offices—all these depend on men. Men indeed accomplish their work through methods, while methods must await men to put them into practice. Thus, to implement methods of government, one must cultivate civil affairs to spread the virtue that wins allegiance through kindness, and organize military affairs to display the might of punitive expeditions. The achievements of securing peace within and repelling threats from without will then be realized together. To obtain men who can govern, one must take benevolence as the foundation, broadening the impartiality with which talent is welcomed, and fully exercise wisdom, making clear the standards for distinguishing merit. Upon these one constantly depends for achievements in assisting government and carrying forward the ruler’s transforming influence. Since antiquity, in ages of great peace, the ruler has enjoyed ease above while ministers have labored below; the four quarters have turned toward his influence, and the remotest regions have followed his standards. This has depended on possessing these means. Otherwise, although there may be a benevolent and sagely sovereign above, there are no loyal and worthy assistants below; although the ruler may aspire to good government, the people cannot receive the blessings of consummate rule. Not only do offices lack the right men, but methods consequently also fail to be implemented. How, then, could one dispense with means of changing this situation?

I reverently consider that Your Majesty the Emperor, endowed with sagacity, spiritual insight, and civil and military accomplishments, has established the supreme standard of benevolence, righteousness, centrality, and rectitude. Reverently comporting yourself and letting your robes hang down, you …

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
辟欽承動容作色而海内震恐四十餘年之
間三辰軌度九域奠維以天地則既泰矣塗
歌里誦嶽貢川輸以民物則既阜矣賓琛交
貢玉帛来同以戎狄則賓矣然猶
聖不自聖進臣等于
廷諮以當世之務斯心也視民如傷之心望道
未見之心也臣誠愚陋不足以塞
大問應
明旨雖然敢不掇拾所聞而對揚萬一乎臣伏讀
聖制首稱堯舜無為之治繼之以宣王中興之烈
===
且嘉慕當時之諸臣而歎今之不然臣有以
仰窺
聖意而得其說矣夫唐虞之世雖稱治安然洚水
警余猶切其咨之慮有苗弗率不免徂征之
師卒之四隩宅而洚水平兩階舞而有苗格
何其不勞而成功之若是也盖當是時有禹
益諸臣一德一心以修輔厥后而二聖人者
特垂拱仰成爾已周宣之世雖稱中興然觀
雲漢鴻鴈諸詩則民人未必其盡安觀采薇
六月諸詩則方内未必其無警卒之海宇臻

且嘉慕當時之諸臣而歎今之不然臣有以
===
仰窺
聖意而得其說矣夫唐虞之世雖稱治安然洚水
警余猶切其咨之慮有苗弗率不免徂征之
師夅之四隩宅而洚水平兩階舞而有苗格
何其不勞而成功之若是也蓋當是時有禹
益諸臣一德一心以修輔厥后而二聖人者
特垂拱仰成爾已周宣之世雖稱中興然觀
雲漢鴻鴈諸詩則民人未必其盡安觀采薇
六月諸詩則方內未必其無警卒之海宇臻
punctuated:
辟欽承，動容作色而海内震恐。四十餘年之間，三辰軌度，九域奠維，以天地則既泰矣；塗歌里誦，嶽貢川輸，以民物則既阜矣；賓琛交貢，玉帛来同，以戎狄則賓矣。然猶聖不自聖，進臣等于廷，諮以當世之務。斯心也，視民如傷之心，望道未見之心也。臣誠愚陋，不足以塞大問、應明旨。雖然，敢不掇拾所聞而對揚萬一乎？臣伏讀聖制，首稱堯舜無為之治，繼之以宣王中興之烈，且嘉慕當時之諸臣，而歎今之不然。臣有以仰窺聖意而得其說矣。
夫唐虞之世，雖稱治安，然「洚水警余」，猶切其咨之慮；有苗弗率，不免徂征之師。卒之四隩宅而洚水平，兩階舞而有苗格。何其不勞而成功之若是也？盖當是時，有禹、益諸臣，一德一心，以修輔厥后，而二聖人者，特垂拱仰成爾已。周宣之世，雖稱中興，然觀《雲漢》《鴻鴈》諸詩，則民人未必其盡安；觀《采薇》《六月》諸詩，則方内未必其無警。卒之海宇臻
translation_en:
…the assembled officials reverently obey; at a change in Your Majesty’s expression or demeanor, all within the seas tremble in awe. Over more than forty years, the sun, moon, and stars have followed their courses, and the foundations of the nine regions have been secured: Heaven and Earth have attained harmony. Songs rise along the roads and praises in the villages; tribute comes from the mountains and goods are conveyed along the rivers: the people and material resources have attained abundance. Precious offerings from foreign visitors arrive in succession, and bearers of jade and silk come together at court: the Rong and Di have submitted as guests. Yet, sage though You are, You do not regard Yourself as a sage. You have brought us, Your servants, into court and consulted us on the affairs of the present age. This is the heart that cares for the people as though they were injured, that looks toward the Way as though it had not yet been seen. Your servant is truly ignorant and uncultivated, incapable of adequately answering Your great question or responding to Your enlightened instructions. Nevertheless, dare I fail to gather what I have heard and offer a reply that gives expression to even a tiny part of Your intent? Your servant has reverently read Your sacred decree. It first praises the effortless government of Yao and Shun, then the achievements of King Xuan’s restoration; it also expresses admiration for the ministers of those times and laments that things are otherwise today. From this, Your servant has been able respectfully to discern Your sacred intent and grasp its meaning.
Although the age of Tang and Yu was celebrated for good government and peace, the words “The flood waters alarm me” still express the urgent anxiety behind the ruler’s consultations. When the Youmiao would not obey, a military expedition could not be avoided. In the end, the lands in all four quarters became habitable and the flood waters subsided; a dance between the two stairways brought the Youmiao to submit. How could such achievements have been accomplished without toil? It was because at that time ministers such as Yu and Yi, united in virtue and purpose, diligently assisted their sovereigns; the two sages merely sat with folded hands and relied upon their accomplishments. Although the reign of King Xuan of Zhou was celebrated as a restoration, reading such poems as “The Milky Way” and “The Wild Geese” shows that the people were not necessarily all at peace; reading such poems as “Gathering Bracken” and “The Sixth Month” shows that the realm was not necessarily free of alarms. text:
富庶之休夷狄底蕩平之績又何其不勞而
成功之若是也盖當是時有吉甫方叔諸臣
矢心戮力以弘濟時艱而宣王特委任責成
爾已所以然者豈堯舜宣王無憂天下之心
而專屬之臣與盖人君所履者天位也所治
者天職也天何言哉以一氣運於上而四時
五行為之節宣於其間者分也君何為哉以
一德宰於上而百司庶府為之協理於其下
者亦分也唐虞成周之世君法天道而總攬
以馭其臣臣代天工而勤職以事其君此所

後世垂休良有以也由是觀之水旱盜賊之
災固不足以為盛世之累其所以斡旋氣化
保衛生靈者則在乎奮庸熈載之有人而折
衝禦侮之有賴耳洪惟我
太祖高皇帝肇造區宇丕顯之謨無以加矣然軍
旅之後旱暵相仍而湖南辰貴之間時猶揚
塵鳴鏑屢犯王誅則水旱盜賊之警不盡無

之經理其文事外有徐常諸臣為之振揚其

…the blessings of wealth and abundance, and the achievement of pacifying the Yi and Di peoples—how, again, could such success have been achieved without toil? It was because ministers such as Jifu and Fang Shu then pledged their hearts and joined their efforts to overcome the difficulties of the age, while King Xuan merely entrusted them with responsibility and held them accountable for success. Was this because Yao, Shun, and King Xuan had no concern for the realm and left it entirely to their ministers? The position occupied by the ruler is Heaven’s position; the duties he administers are Heaven’s duties. What does Heaven say? A single vital force circulates above, while the four seasons and five phases regulate and diffuse it in their midst: this is the division of responsibilities. What does the ruler do? A single virtue governs above, while the many offices and bureaus cooperate in administering affairs below: this, too, is the division of responsibilities. In the ages of Tang, Yu, and the established Zhou order, rulers modeled themselves on Heaven’s Way and exercised overall control over their ministers; ministers performed Heaven’s work, diligently fulfilling their duties in service to their rulers. Thus calamities and baleful influences became auspicious blessings, and war chariots gave way to jade and silk offered in peace. There was good reason why their contemporaries praised these sage rulers and later generations inherited their blessings. Viewed in this light, the calamities of floods, droughts, and banditry need not impair a flourishing age. The means of guiding the transformations of vital force and protecting living people depend on having men who exert their abilities and bring their tasks to fruition, and on having those upon whom one can rely to repel attacks and resist aggression.
We reverently consider how our Taizu, the Exalted Emperor, founded the realm: nothing could surpass his splendid designs. Yet after the military campaigns, drought followed drought, and in the region of Hunan, Chen, and Gui [?], dust still rose and arrows still whistled, repeatedly provoking imperial punishment. text:

太祖不勞而天下治也
成祖文皇帝中靖家邦丕承之烈無以加矣然北
方阻饑江南大水而日本安南之寇時猶虓
闞内覬擾我中華則水旱盗賊之警亦不盡
無也然而民不稱病者則以文有楊夏之徒
宣力於中朝武有劉朱之屬揚威於外徼故
我
成祖不勞而天下治也

武威，故我太祖不勞而天下治也。
成祖文皇帝中靖家邦，丕承之烈無以加矣。然北方阻饑，江南大水，而日本、安南之寇時猶虓闞内覬，擾我中華，則水旱盗賊之警亦不盡無也。然而民不稱病者，則以文有楊、夏之徒宣力於中朝，武有劉、朱之屬揚威於外徼，故我成祖不勞而天下治也。

translation_en:
…military might; thus our Emperor Taizu governed All-under-Heaven without exertion.
Emperor Chengzu Wen pacified the imperial house and realm within; his achievement in magnificently carrying forward the inheritance could not be surpassed. Yet the north suffered famine, Jiangnan experienced great floods, and raiders from Japan and Annan still at times roared menacingly and cast covetous eyes inward, troubling our central realm. Thus alarms over floods, droughts, and banditry were not entirely absent. Nevertheless, the people did not complain of distress, because civil servants such as Yang and Xia exerted themselves at the central court, while military men such as Liu and Zhu displayed their might on the outer frontiers. Thus our Emperor Chengzu governed All-under-Heaven without exertion.
The successive sage emperors inherited the throne, and the transforming influence of peace grew ever more abundant and pervasive. Although their ordering of civil and military affairs originated in the independent workings of their profound imperial minds, the contributions of those who assisted in government and carried forward that transforming influence cannot be denied.
Your servant humbly observes that, since ascending the throne, Your Majesty has revered Heaven and followed the example of your ancestors, daring to neglect no matter; you have cultivated virtue and attended diligently to government, relaxing not even for a moment. Thus, whenever rain and sunshine in the capital region failed to arrive in their proper seasons, you personally offered prayers at the altar of purification in advance. As soon as news arrived of floods or droughts in the prefectures and counties, you promptly provided relief without delay. As for dispatching military provisions to Datong, this arose especially from your sagacious planning; in commuting payments in kind in Suzhou and Songjiang, you graciously accommodated the officials’ proposals. translation_en:
…must invariably reach him. Concerned about armed resistance in Min and Guang, he consults and deliberates tirelessly. His benevolent heart and benevolent government truly rival those of Tang and Yu and surpass those of the Zhou at its height, without his resting upon these achievements [?]. Surely, then, officials ought to perform their duties adequately and the people live in peace; moral transformation ought to flourish and customs be good; the foundations of the state ought to be secure within, with no disasters or portents arising; and the state's might ought to extend abroad, with no need to resort to arms. Yet recently the common people have suffered famine, while the rebels in the south have grown increasingly rampant. Seasons and years have passed without relief from Your Majesty's anxiety. Your servant is deeply perplexed by this. Having privately reflected at length upon its causes, I believe that, although Your Majesty's concern for the people is earnest, those charged with transmitting and carrying out your benevolent intentions may include many selfish, self-seeking ministers. Although Your Majesty diligently strives to suppress disorder, those charged with upholding and displaying your august authority may not be men who serve loyally and exert their strength. This is why your beneficence has not reached everywhere and effective government has not yet been achieved.
Your servant has heard that success in securing peace within and repelling threats from without depends solely upon civil and military service; and those entrusted with civil and military responsibilities are generals and officials. The plans by which the sage emperors and enlightened kings of antiquity achieved enduring peace and lasting good government all followed this principle. Leaving aside the ages before Tang and Yu, the Rites of Zhou records Storekeepers (yiren), who managed the stockpiled provisions of the counties and domains to prepare for famine; Granary Directors (linren), who kept account of the nine grains to report abundance or scarcity; District Preceptors (xiangshi), who made seasonal rounds among the people; and Directors of Relief (sijiu), who distributed aid by royal command. Above them were ministers charged with spreading benevolent and harmonious government, who tended the common people day and night and reported their administration to the court. Thus the responsibility for securing the people's peace was borne by ministers, and the ruler did not undertake it himself. Investigating wrongdoing was entrusted to the Chief Judicial Officers (shishi), and examining cases of killing to the Court Officers (chaoshi). There were Directors of Convict Labor (sili) to apprehend robbers and Patrol Officers (huanren) to detect them. Above them were ministers dispatched with full military command and entrusted with authority over their own theaters of operations, who day and night…

整齊其卒伍，而折衝于邊鄙，則遏亂之責，臣寔任之，而君亦不自為也。君不自為而臣為之，臣代君為而君任之，勞逸各得其所，而文武咸盡其才，欲天下無治，不可得也。
今之結綬分符，為陛下之吏者，陛下固亦以安民責之矣。而夷考其人，果能如伏湛之分俸賑民乎？果能如夏侯惇之斷水作陂乎？果能如蔡齊之弛禁利民、王望之開倉救殍乎？有之，或弗克自效，而竭澤為漁以富私橐者相望也。甚則水旱不以實聞，增損委之胥吏，而百姓嗷然，有思亂之心矣。
今之擁旄秉鉞，為陛下之將者，陛下固亦以遏亂責之矣。而於稽其人，果能如張耳之馬箠下城乎？果能如充國之枕席過師乎？果能如李靖之蹀血虜廷、賀若弼之酹酒江上乎？有之，或弗克自奮，而選耎畏懦以糜稟祿者皆是也。甚則擅奪首功，扣除常給，而盜賊蠢然，有輕中國之心矣。夫民窮故盜起
translation_en:
…put their troops in order and repel incursions on the frontiers. Thus ministers truly bear the responsibility for suppressing disorder, and the ruler likewise does not undertake it himself. The ruler does not act himself; his ministers act for him. Ministers act in the ruler’s place, and the ruler entrusts them with their duties. Toil and ease each fall to their proper share, and civil and military officials alike fully employ their talents. Under such circumstances, it would be impossible for the realm to remain ungoverned.
Those who now tie on official seal-ribbons and receive divided tallies of authority, serving as Your Majesty’s officials, have certainly also been charged by Your Majesty with bringing peace to the people. Yet, examining these men impartially, can they really share their salaries to relieve the people as Fu Zhan did? Can they really dam waterways to make reservoirs as Xiahou Dun did? Can they really relax prohibitions to benefit the people as Cai Qi did, or open granaries to save those dying of starvation as Wang Wang did? Some such men exist, but they may be unable to make their service effective, while those who drain the pond to catch its fish, enriching their own purses, are everywhere to be seen. Worse still, they fail to report floods and droughts truthfully, leaving increases and reductions in the reported figures to subordinate clerks. The common people cry out in distress and begin to contemplate rebellion.
Those who now bear yak-tail standards and wield battle-axes of command, serving as Your Majesty’s generals, have certainly also been charged by Your Majesty with suppressing disorder. Yet, upon examining these men [?], can they really take cities with a riding whip as Zhang Er did? Can they really move an army with the ease of resting on a pillow and mat as Chongguo did [?]? Can they really tread through blood in the enemy’s court as Li Jing did, or pour a libation of wine beside the Yangzi as He Ruobi did? Some such men exist, but they may be unable to exert themselves, while those who are weak, fearful, and cowardly, squandering their stipends, are everywhere. Worse still, they arbitrarily appropriate credit for enemy heads taken and withhold regular provisions. The bandits stir into activity and begin to hold the Central Realm in contempt. For when the people are impoverished, banditry arises…

…Once banditry arises, the people become still poorer. A shortage of food brings military operations, and military operations deepen the shortage of food. When offices are held by the wrong men, the laws become corrupted; once the laws are corrupted, remedying them becomes still harder. This is why the sage Son of Heaven sits in anxious anticipation of worthy talent, slaps his thigh in longing for commanders, wistfully contemplates government through nonaction, and sighs that the present falls so far short of antiquity. Whatever direction the mind takes, all the limbs obey its commands; whatever the sovereign desires, all his officials vie to pursue. Consider the selection of civil officials. Those who are calm and sincere are sometimes faulted for lacking literary refinement; those who exhaust themselves caring for the people are sometimes reproached for clumsy administration. Yet those appointed through examination success are not lightly subjected to impeachment; those whose accounts and documents are in order may be tolerated despite their weakness and ineffectiveness; and those adept at serving their superiors escape public punishment for corruption. When officials throughout the realm see that worthy men are not necessarily advanced and unworthy men are not necessarily dismissed, who will still seek to repay imperial favor with gratitude, discipline his conduct, and establish a good name, aspiring to join the ranks of upright and benevolent officials? title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
市恩則貪殘者稱為忠良卑諂以媚上則畏
懦者附于儒雅虛言以瞽眾則誕妄者信其
雄畧天下之將見有功者未必上而無功者
未必下也誰復有撫劍抵掌出身犯難以求
不負乎干城之寄者哉天下之所以無賢將
帥職此之故也臣聞天生一代之才必足以
供一代之用上有明明之君下必有翼翼之
臣顧所以用之何如耳茲欲選任皆得其人
而文武惟其所用則臣請以仁智之說為
陛下終言之孟軻氏有云智者無不知也當務之
===
為急仁者無不愛也急親賢之為務夫所謂
親賢者非煦煦焉昵比以為恩也以公心選
之以隆禮待之以誠意委之而高爵厚祿有
所不靳寸長小善有所不遺自古帝王所以
顯忠遂良而天下稱至仁者胥此也所謂當
務者非察察焉綜核以為明也辨忠邪之分
稽功罪之實慎賞罰之施而一人之毀譽有
所不恤一己之聰明有所不任自古帝王所
以舉直措枉而天下稱大智者胥此也仁而
匪智則爵賞太濫而奸邪或得以苟容智而

…to buy favor, then the greedy and cruel are acclaimed as loyal and worthy; when men abase themselves and flatter their superiors, the timid and cowardly are ranked among the cultivated and refined; when men blind the multitude with empty words, the boastful and deceitful win belief in their grand strategies. When the generals of the realm see that those with achievements are not necessarily promoted, while those without achievements are not necessarily demoted, who will again grasp his sword and strike his palms together in resolve, risking his life and braving danger, in hopes of fulfilling the trust placed in him as the realm’s shield and rampart? This is precisely why the realm lacks worthy commanders.
Your servant has heard that the talent Heaven produces in any age must suffice for that age’s needs. Where there is an enlightened ruler above, there must be diligent and reverent ministers below; it depends only on how they are employed. If appointments are now to secure the right people in every case, and civil and military talent is to be put to its proper use, your servant begs to conclude his address to Your Majesty with a discussion of benevolence and wisdom. Meng Ke said: “The wise understand all things, but give priority to the tasks that demand attention; the benevolent love all people, but make drawing close to the worthy their urgent task.” Drawing close to the worthy does not mean displaying petty kindness and treating intimate familiarity as a mark of favor. It means selecting them impartially, treating them with the highest ceremonial respect, and entrusting them with responsibilities in sincerity; it means not stinting high rank and generous stipends, and overlooking no modest ability or small virtue. These are the means by which emperors and kings since antiquity have honored the loyal and advanced the worthy, earning the acclaim of the realm for supreme benevolence.
Attending to urgent tasks does not mean scrutinizing and checking every detail and taking this for discernment. It means distinguishing loyalty from treachery, investigating the facts of achievements and offenses, and exercising care in bestowing rewards and punishments; it means being prepared to disregard an individual’s praise or slander and not relying solely on one’s own intelligence. These are the means by which emperors and kings since antiquity have raised up the upright and set aside the crooked, earning the acclaim of the realm for great wisdom. title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
匪仁則推求太過而賢才不樂于嚮用是故
欲為擇吏計則莫若廣選舉之途如古之孝
弟賢良與文學並進可也嚴考課之典如古
之大明黜陟歲終奏舉殿最可也行久任之
法如古之居官長子孫有績則進爵加秩可
也而又申勅銓曹使之選任有司務求端良
修潔之士而儇薄好名者無所容焉將見百
司競勸庶賢彙征旬宣者為曾鞏之去疾廉
謹者為羊續之懸魚雖有水旱之災而困窮
之民且將還定而安集矣唐虞風動之休成
===
周順治之化不可以復見乎欲為擇將計則
莫若畧世裔以求真才如古之起自行陣而
拜為大將者可也專委任以需實效如古之
便宜行事而不從中制者可也信賞罰以勵
頹靡如古之謗書盈篋而不問揮淚斬將而
不恤可也而又嚴責本兵使之選任將帥務
求沉毅果敢之士而庸懦無能者弗得與焉
將見策士效謀勇夫效力督撫者皆良平之
器授鉞者皆韓白之才雖有竊發之警而烏
集之眾且將喙息之不暇矣唐虞來王之化

匪仁，則推求太過，而賢才不樂于嚮用。是故欲為擇吏計，則莫若廣選舉之途，如古之孝弟賢良與文學並進可也；嚴考課之典，如古之大明黜陟、歲終奏舉殿最可也；行久任之法，如古之居官長子孫、有績則進爵加秩可也。而又申勅銓曹，使之選任有司，務求端良修潔之士，而儇薄好名者無所容焉。將見百司競勸，庶賢彙征，旬宣者為曾鞏之去疾，廉謹者為羊續之懸魚。雖有水旱之災，而困窮之民且將還定而安集矣。唐虞風動之休、成周順治之化，不可以復見乎？

欲為擇將計，則莫若畧世裔以求真才，如古之起自行陣而拜為大將者可也；專委任以需實效，如古之便宜行事而不從中制者可也；信賞罰以勵頹靡，如古之謗書盈篋而不問、揮淚斬將而不恤可也。而又嚴責本兵，使之選任將帥，務求沉毅果敢之士，而庸懦無能者弗得與焉。將見策士效謀，勇夫效力，督撫者皆良平之器，授鉞者皆韓白之才。雖有竊發之警，而烏集之眾且將喙息之不暇矣。唐虞來王之化
translation_en:
…without benevolence, scrutiny becomes excessive, and worthy and talented men take no pleasure in entering service. Thus, in planning the selection of civil officials, nothing is better than broadening the avenues of recommendation and selection: one may follow antiquity in advancing men of filial devotion, brotherly respect, worthiness, and goodness alongside men of literary learning. One should make the regulations for evaluating performance rigorous: one may follow antiquity in clearly determining demotions and promotions and submitting reports at year’s end identifying the worst and best performers. One should institute long tenure in office: one may follow antiquity in allowing officials to remain in office long enough to raise children and grandchildren, advancing their noble titles and official ranks when they achieve results. Further, renewed injunctions should be issued to the personnel authorities that, in selecting and appointing administrative officials, they must seek upright, good men of cultivated and unsullied character, leaving no place for the frivolous and shallow who crave fame. Then we shall see officials in every bureau striving to distinguish themselves, and worthy men advancing together. Those charged with proclaiming imperial instruction throughout their jurisdictions will remove afflictions as Zeng Gong did; those of incorruptible and conscientious conduct will emulate Yang Xu in hanging up the fish offered to him. Even amid floods and droughts, the impoverished people will regain stability and settle in peace. Could we not witness once again the blessings of the transforming influence of Tang and Yu, and the orderly governance of the flourishing Zhou?

In planning the selection of generals, nothing is better than setting aside hereditary descent to seek genuine talent: one may follow antiquity in appointing men who rose from the ranks as great generals. One should entrust them with undivided authority and await tangible results: one may follow antiquity in allowing them to act as circumstances require, without control from within the court. One should make rewards and punishments trustworthy so as to rouse the dispirited: one may follow antiquity in leaving a chestful of defamatory letters unexamined, yet shedding tears as one executes a general without allowing pity to intervene. Further, the Minister of War should be held strictly responsible for selecting and appointing commanders, seeking men who are composed, resolute, and courageous, and excluding the mediocre, cowardly, and incompetent. Then we shall see strategists contributing their plans and brave men exerting their strength. Supreme commanders and grand coordinators will all possess the capacity of Zhang Liang and Chen Ping; those invested with the battle-axe of command will all possess the talent of Han Xin and Bai Qi. Even should sudden outbreaks raise the alarm, those crowds gathered like crows will not have a moment to catch their breath. The transforming influence of Tang and Yu, which brought distant peoples to acknowledge their kingship…

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
周室干襄之威又不可以復見乎要之廣求
賢才以備國家之用者皆仁也旌别淑慝以
昭勸懲之典者皆智也仁以運乎其智故内
外文武之臣咸欣欣焉戴
陛下之恩而不忍自負乎知遇之隆智以濟乎其
仁故内外文武之臣咸兢兢焉畏
陛下之明而不敢自蹈于欺罔之咎由是而民安
寇息由是而災消祥降萬世治平之業恒必
賴之矣抑臣又聞之圖事者貴謀之于豫而
斂才者貴養之于初今
===
朝廷以科貢取士士固多良矣然飾文華而鮮
為已之功爭進取而乏恬退之節者亦時時

…and the martial awe of the Zhou royal house [?]—could these not be seen again? In sum, seeking worthy and talented men widely to meet the needs of the state is entirely a matter of benevolence; distinguishing the good from the wicked to make clear the standards of encouragement and punishment is entirely a matter of wisdom. When benevolence directs that wisdom, civil and military officials both at court and in the provinces will all joyfully acknowledge Your Majesty’s favor, unable to bear betraying the great kindness of being recognized and employed. When wisdom assists that benevolence, those officials will all stand in reverent fear of Your Majesty’s discernment, not daring to incur the guilt of deceit. Through this the people will be secure and banditry will cease; through this calamities will vanish and auspicious signs descend. The enterprise of securing peace and good government for ten thousand generations must always depend upon this. Moreover, your servant has heard that in planning affairs, what matters is to deliberate beforehand, and in gathering talent, what matters is to nurture it from the outset.
The court now recruits scholars through the examinations and tribute recommendation system, and certainly many of them are worthy. Yet there are also, from time to time, those who embellish their literary expression but do little to cultivate themselves [?], and who compete for advancement but lack the integrity to remain content in retirement. Moral instruction must therefore be strengthened. I request that the teachings of the Way be clearly expounded in schools throughout the realm, and that men of upright and pure conduct be chosen to head them. Let students attain a clear understanding and firm observance of the principles of filial devotion, fraternal respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness, and of the virtues of integrity, a sense of shame, ritual propriety, and deference. Only then should they be recruited through the examinations and tribute recommendation system and entrusted with responsibility for the people and the altars of the soil. Thus, learning in youth and putting their learning into practice in maturity, they need not fear lacking the means to govern. Thoroughly studying the classics and applying their learning, they will be able to extend their understanding to other matters. With this accomplished, there would be no cause to worry that the realm lacked good officials.
The court selects generals through the military examinations, and certainly many of them are worthy. Yet there are also those whose strength suffices to draw a powerful bow, but whose practical application is deficient; whose eloquence suffices to alert the ignorant, but who fall into confusion whenever confronted with affairs …

進退之方虛實堅瑕之勢耳習所聞目熟所
見然後試之以武舉而授之以鈇鉞之任則
籌敵制勝洞如指掌戡亂鋤奸易若轉樞如
是而憂將之不良者未之有也將良矣吏良
矣天下無事
陛下無憂矣
萬幾閒暇之際
九重深邃之中其將何所事事乎臣聞天下國家
===
之本在人君一心而已自此心之至公則為
仁自此心之至明則為智以是至公至明之
心而乂安天下則文德修以是至公至明之
心而肅清天下則武功振斯道也
陛下敬一之箴固已該括而無餘矣臣愚芹曝之
私惟願益新
聖德祗慎厥終盛滿弗矜則為舜之無怠無荒幽
獨必謹則為文之亦臨亦保立綱陳紀則守
之以不愆不忘之訓任賢去邪則决之以勿
疑勿貳之明察天人理欲之幾則不邇不殖

translation_en:
…such cases also occur from time to time; training therefore demands careful attention. I ask that additional military schools be established in the prefectures and counties throughout the realm, and that men thoroughly versed in military strategy be chosen as their instructors. Let students become familiar, through hearing and seeing, with the methods of sitting, rising, advancing, and retreating, and with dispositions of weakness and strength, solidity and vulnerability. Then examine them through the military examinations and entrust them with military command, symbolized by the battle-axe. They will understand how to assess the enemy and secure victory as clearly as they see their own palms; suppressing rebellion and rooting out evildoers will be as easy as turning a pivot. With matters thus arranged, there has never been reason to fear a lack of capable generals. With capable generals and capable civil officials, the realm will be free of trouble, and Your Majesty free of worry.
In moments of leisure amid the myriad affairs of government, within the secluded depths of the imperial palace, to what, then, should Your Majesty devote yourself? Your servant has heard that the foundation of the realm and the state lies solely in the ruler’s heart. Its utmost impartiality constitutes benevolence; its utmost clarity constitutes wisdom. When this utterly impartial and clear heart is employed to govern and pacify the realm, civil virtue is cultivated; when it is employed to purge the realm of disorder, military achievement flourishes. Your Majesty’s Admonition on Reverent Unity already comprehensively embraces this Way, leaving nothing out. Yet your foolish servant, in the humble spirit of one offering celery or the warmth of the sun, wishes only that Your Majesty continually renew your sagely virtue and remain reverently attentive to the end. If, at the height of prosperity, you refrain from pride, you will embody Shun’s freedom from indolence and negligence. If you remain vigilant even in solitude, you will embody King Wen’s sense of being watched over and protected. In establishing the guiding principles and setting forth the rules, uphold the injunction to ‘neither transgress nor forget.’ In employing the worthy and dismissing the wicked, decide with the clarity that permits ‘neither doubt nor divided purpose.’ In discerning the subtle junctures between Heaven and humanity, and between moral principle and desire, then ‘neither draw near [to pleasures] nor accumulate [wealth]’…

未危未亂之防常惺然於吾之念將見百官

之戒常惕然於吾之心；考古今得失之監，則未危未亂之防常惺然於吾之念。將見百官庶吏莫不精白以承休，而細奸小醜亦且回心而向善。恩從祥風翔，德與和氣游，上以答天心之景貺，下以綿國脉于靈長。董子所謂「君心正而福祥集」，詩所謂「天保定爾，亦孔之固」，且為今日頌之矣。至治盛，豈特比隆虞周而已哉！
疎狂之論，不識忌諱，無任隕越之至。臣謹對。
translation_en:
…the admonition will remain a constant warning in Your Majesty’s heart. In examining the lessons of successes and failures, ancient and modern, precautions taken before danger or disorder arises will remain ever present in Your Majesty’s thoughts. Then we shall see all officials and subordinate functionaries purify themselves to receive your beneficence, while even petty miscreants and insignificant villains will turn their hearts toward goodness. Your grace will soar with auspicious winds, and your virtue will move with harmonious vital energies: above, responding to the great blessings bestowed by Heaven’s heart; below, prolonging the dynasty’s lifeblood into an auspicious and enduring future. Master Dong’s saying, “When the ruler’s heart is upright, blessings and auspicious signs gather,” and the words of the Book of Odes, “Heaven protects and establishes you; how very firm you are,” will serve as praises of this very day. Could the flourishing of such perfect governance merely equal the grandeur of the reign of Shun and the Zhou dynasty?
In this reckless discourse, I have failed to heed taboos and can scarcely contain my profound fear and trembling. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
臣余有丁
臣對臣聞人君代天以理物常秉天下之大
權以成無爲之治人臣代君以協理當明天
下之大分以建匪懈之功何也君之尊猶天
也操乾綱以獨斷於上一乾元之統天焉而
凝神端拱於以享其逸而不勞臣之事君猶
事天也守坤貞以疏附於下一坤順之承天
焉而竭力圖惟於以任其勞而不避君享其
逸匪自豫也無心而成化天道本如是也人
君奉若天道巍然臨御於九重而委任以責
===
之臣焉斯有以得大君之宜臣任其勞匪自
瘁也無成而代終地道本如是也人臣效法
地道夔然恪共乎庶職而盡忠以效之君焉
斯有以得純臣之義惟君以天自處是能以
天之心爲心也故其治足以則乎天而聖帝
明王不能外是以近恭默之衡惟臣以天事
君是能以君之心爲心也故其忠足以孚乎
君而賢相忠臣不能外是以奏協恭之績君
臣得而萬化行所以亮采惠疇者有全功上
下交而庶務理所以謨明弼諧者有偉烈渾

臣余有丁。
臣對：臣聞人君代天以理物，常秉天下之大權，以成無爲之治；人臣代君以協理，當明天下之大分，以建匪懈之功。何也？君之尊猶天也，操乾綱以獨斷於上，一乾元之統天焉，而凝神端拱，於以享其逸而不勞。臣之事君猶事天也，守坤貞以疏附於下，一坤順之承天焉，而竭力圖惟，於以任其勞而不避。君享其逸，匪自豫也，無心而成化，天道本如是也。人君奉若天道，巍然臨御於九重，而委任以責之臣焉，斯有以得大君之宜。臣任其勞，匪自瘁也，無成而代終，地道本如是也。人臣效法地道，夔然恪共乎庶職，而盡忠以效之君焉，斯有以得純臣之義。惟君以天自處，是能以天之心爲心也，故其治足以則乎天，而聖帝明王不能外是以近恭默之衡。惟臣以天事君，是能以君之心爲心也，故其忠足以孚乎君，而賢相忠臣不能外是以奏協恭之績。君臣得而萬化行，所以亮采惠疇者有全功；上下交而庶務理，所以謨明弼諧者有偉烈。渾
translation_en:
Your servant, Yu Youding.
Your servant replies: I have heard that the ruler acts on Heaven’s behalf in ordering all things, always wielding the great authority of the realm to achieve government through nonaction. Ministers assist in governing on the ruler’s behalf and should clearly understand the fundamental distinctions of station in the realm, so as to accomplish their work without slackening. Why is this? The ruler’s exalted position resembles Heaven’s. He holds the guiding power of Qian, the Creative, and decides alone above, wholly resembling the primal power of Qian in its command of Heaven. Concentrating his spirit and sitting upright with hands folded, he thus enjoys ease without toil. Ministers serve their ruler as they serve Heaven. Maintaining the steadfastness of Kun, the Receptive, they remain closely attached to him below, wholly resembling Kun’s obedience in supporting Heaven. Exerting all their strength in planning and deliberation, they undertake their labors without shirking.
The ruler enjoys ease, but not for his own pleasure: transformation is accomplished without deliberate intention, for such is inherently the Way of Heaven. The ruler follows and accords with Heaven’s Way, presiding majestically within the ninefold palace, delegating responsibilities to his ministers and holding them accountable. Thus he fulfills what befits a great ruler. Ministers undertake toil, but not simply to exhaust themselves: claiming no achievement of their own, they bring affairs to completion on another’s behalf, for such is inherently the Way of Earth. Ministers model themselves upon Earth’s Way, reverently and conscientiously attending to their various offices and devoting their utmost loyalty to serving their ruler. Thus they fulfill the duty of wholly devoted ministers.
Only when the ruler takes Heaven as the model for his own position can he make Heaven’s heart his own. His government can therefore accord with Heaven; even sage emperors and enlightened kings cannot depart from this in approaching the standard of reverent silence [?]. Only when ministers serve their ruler as Heaven can they make the ruler’s heart their own. Their loyalty can therefore win their ruler’s trust; even worthy chief ministers and loyal servants cannot depart from this in achieving harmonious and reverent service. When ruler and ministers fulfill their proper roles, all transformations proceed, and their efforts to assist in affairs and duly order the various categories of business achieve complete success. When those above and below communicate, the manifold affairs are put in order, and clear counsel and harmonious assistance produce great accomplishments. An unspoiled…

悉心陳列勿憚勿欺也顧臣愚陋猥謭何所
知識得以少裨
大廷之對而
陛下厤德之萬一乎然恭承
溫旨仰體
淵衷敢不披瀝誠悃以對臣聞之書曰天佑下民
作之君師以對上帝是天之所以寵綏乎君
punctuated: 噩純庬之風可以坐致，雍熈悠久之業自兹有成矣。欽惟皇帝陛下，稟神聖之資，撫熈明之運，敬一紹帝王之道統，倫制立古今之治極，恭黙通於上載，聲教布於遐陬。禮樂明備，而大車書一統之盛；華夏率俾，而洽干羽兩階之休。嘉靖萬邦，迄今四十有一年如一日矣。臣竊伏草茅，幸際陛下久道成化，壽考作人，叨與有司之選，親承大廷之對。而清問下及，首焉嘉慕帝王致治之盛，既而軫念災寇荐至之警，深有慨於文武庶職之難其人焉。將求弭變以安民，遏亂以固本，且責臣等悉心陳列，勿憚勿欺也。顧臣愚陋猥譾，何所知識，得以少裨陛下麻德之萬一乎？然恭承温旨，仰體淵衷，敢不披瀝誠悃以對？臣聞之，《書》曰：「天佑下民，作之君師，以對上帝。」是天之所以寵綏乎君……
translation_en:
…a spirit of pristine simplicity and purity can readily be brought about, and an enduring achievement of harmony and prosperity will thus be accomplished.

Reverently considering Your Majesty the Emperor: endowed with sagely and divine qualities, you preside over an age of radiant enlightenment. Through reverence and unity of purpose, you continue the transmission of the Way of emperors and kings; through ordered relationships and institutions, you establish the highest standard of government for all ages. Your reverent silence communes with Heaven’s workings, and your civilizing influence reaches the remotest corners. Rites and music are manifest and complete, magnifying the splendor of a realm unified in carriage gauges and written script. The people of Huaxia all submit, universally sharing the blessing symbolized by the dance with shields and plumes between the two stairways. You have brought good order and peace to the myriad realms; through forty-one years down to the present, your constancy has been as that of a single day.

Your servant, dwelling obscurely among the common people, has fortunately encountered Your Majesty’s enduring practice of the Way and transforming influence, your longevity and cultivation of worthy men. Undeservedly selected by the responsible officials, I have personally received the opportunity to answer at the great court. Your august questions have reached down to us. First, you expressed admiration for the splendid government achieved by the emperors and kings; then you voiced anxious concern over the warnings of recurrent disasters and banditry, deeply lamenting the difficulty of finding suitable men for the various civil and military offices. You seek to avert calamities so as to bring peace to the people, and to check disorder so as to secure the foundations of the realm. Moreover, you charge us to set forth our views wholeheartedly, neither shrinking back nor deceiving you. Yet your servant is ignorant, uncultivated, and shallow: what knowledge could I possess that might contribute even the slightest fraction to Your Majesty’s virtue [?; the transcription reads 麻德]? Nevertheless, reverently receiving your gracious instructions and looking up to comprehend your profound intentions, how could I dare not lay bare my sincere feelings in reply?

Your servant has heard it stated in the Book of Documents: “Heaven aids the people below, providing them with rulers and teachers to act in service to the Lord on High.” Thus, Heaven’s favoring and sustaining of the ruler…

寳握中樞位曰天位焉膺歷數纘帝極統曰
天統焉以至心代天意口代天言身代天事
莫非天也則當以天自處矣禮曰惟王建國
設官分職以為民極是君之所以委任乎臣
而臣之所以承命於君者責有歸也故論定
而爵以馭其貴惟君所詔焉位定而祿以馭
其富惟君所予焉以至治君之民理君之事
分君之憂莫非君也則當以天事君矣夫以
一人而欽承昊天之明命一日萬幾不能獨

下同於臣則耳目不逮志慮未周而欲帝載

而君之所以受命於天者，意有在也。故體天寳，握中樞，位曰天位焉；膺歷數，纘帝極，統曰天統焉。以至心代天意，口代天言，身代天事，莫非天也，則當以天自處矣。《禮》曰：「惟王建國，設官分職，以為民極。」是君之所以委任乎臣，而臣之所以承命於君者，責有歸也。故論定而爵，以馭其貴，惟君所詔焉；位定而祿，以馭其富，惟君所予焉。以至治君之民，理君之事，分君之憂，莫非君也，則當以天事君矣。
夫以一人而欽承昊天之明命，一日萬幾，不能獨理，后克艱厥后矣。使日孜孜焉，政事是親，以下同於臣，則耳目不逮，志慮未周，而欲帝載之咸熙也，其可得乎？以一身而奉若天子之明威，百僚庶府，各有專成，臣克艱厥臣矣。使徒泄泄然，尸素是安，以上負其君，則職業不修，機務不理，而欲臣紀之罔虧也，其可得乎？
