translation_en:
…and there is a purpose in the ruler’s receiving Heaven’s mandate. Thus, embodying Heaven’s treasure [?] and holding the central pivot, he occupies a position called the heavenly position; receiving the allotted succession and continuing the imperial rule, he inherits a succession called the heavenly succession. His mind expresses Heaven’s intent, his mouth speaks Heaven’s words, and his person performs Heaven’s work. Since all of this pertains to Heaven, he should conduct himself as Heaven’s representative. The Rites says: “The king establishes the state, creates offices, and distributes duties, thereby setting a standard for the people.” Thus, when the ruler entrusts responsibilities to his ministers and the ministers receive commands from the ruler, responsibility has its proper resting place. Once their merits have been assessed, ranks are conferred to regulate their standing: these depend entirely on the ruler’s commands. Once their positions have been determined, stipends are assigned to regulate their wealth: these depend entirely on the ruler’s grants. They govern the ruler’s people, manage the ruler’s affairs, and share the ruler’s cares. Since all of this pertains to the ruler, they should serve him as they would Heaven.
Now, the ruler, as a single person, reverently receives August Heaven’s illustrious mandate. Each day brings ten thousand matters requiring judgment, which he cannot manage alone: the sovereign must recognize the difficulty of being a sovereign. If he were to toil diligently every day, attending personally to all affairs of government and thereby descending to perform the same tasks as his ministers, his eyes and ears could not reach everything, nor could his deliberations encompass it all. Could he then hope for every imperial undertaking to flourish? A minister, in his own person, reverently obeys the Son of Heaven’s august authority. The many officials and offices each have their particular responsibilities to fulfill: the minister must recognize the difficulty of being a minister. If ministers merely drifted along, content to hold office and draw stipends without doing their work, thereby failing their ruler above, their official duties would go unfulfilled and essential affairs would remain unattended. Could they then hope that the proper order of ministerial service would suffer no impairment?
Looking back to antiquity, none surpassed Yao and Shun in imperial greatness. They indeed brought government through effortless moral influence to its height. Yet at the outset, floodwaters rose to the heavens, and they sought to bring them under control; the common people struggled to obtain food, and they sought to secure their well-being; the Miao would not submit, and they sought to bring them into allegiance. title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
洪水則有禹以底平成若教稼穡則有稷以
粒烝民若明刑罰則有皐陶以弼教化曰翼
為曰明聽各效其職於中天之際而凡政有
未修德有未正用有未利當時諸臣皆有以
代其終是以堯舜得享無為之逸而協和而
風動古今稱極治者唐虞為莫及焉語王之
賢者莫過於周宣固嘗建中興之業矣而其
始焉淮夷是叛思以討之荆蠻為讐思以征
之玁狁匪茹思以伐之而宣王亦未嘗自勞
也誦詩而得采薇諸章若平淮夷則有旬宣
===
之召伯若征荆蠻則有元老之方叔若伐玁
狁則有文武之吉甫曰奔奏曰禦侮各展其
能於多事之日而凡王賦之未進車徒之未
實綜理之未周當時諸臣皆有以共其職是
以宣王得享不勞之治而順治而威嚴古今
稱中興者成周為難繼焉嗣是而降無翼為
明聽之臣安望治之比隆於二帝無奔奏禦
侮之臣安望治之駕美於周王耶是宜
陛下嘉之慕之而陋三代以降於不足言也惟我
陛下篤明禋之敬而心孚

之召伯若征荆蠻則有元老之方叔若伐玁
狁則有文武之吉甫曰奔奏曰禦侮各展其

以宣王得享不勞之治而順治而威嚴古今
稱中興者成周爲難繼焉嗣是而降無翼爲
明聽之臣安望治之比隆於二帝無奔奏禦
侮之臣安望治之駕美於周王耶是宜
陛下嘉之慕之而陋三代以降於不足言也惟我
陛下篤明禋之敬而心乎
punctuated:
洪水，則有禹以底平成；若教稼穡，則有稷以粒烝民；若明刑罰，則有皐陶以弼教化。曰翼為，曰明聽，各效其職於中天之際，而凡政有未修、德有未正、用有未利，當時諸臣皆有以代其終。是以堯舜得享無為之逸，而協和，而風動。古今稱極治者，唐虞為莫及焉。
語王之賢者，莫過於周宣，固嘗建中興之業矣。而其始焉，淮夷是叛，思以討之；荆蠻為讐，思以征之；玁狁匪茹，思以伐之。而宣王亦未嘗自勞也。誦《詩》而得《采薇》諸章，若平淮夷，則有旬宣之召伯；若征荆蠻，則有元老之方叔；若伐玁狁，則有文武之吉甫。曰奔奏，曰禦侮，各展其能於多事之日，而凡王賦之未進、車徒之未實、綜理之未周，當時諸臣皆有以共其職。是以宣王得享不勞之治，而順治，而威嚴。古今稱中興者，成周為難繼焉。
嗣是而降，無翼為明聽之臣，安望治之比隆於二帝？無奔奏禦侮之臣，安望治之駕美於周王耶？是宜陛下嘉之慕之，而陋三代以降於不足言也。惟我陛下篤明禋之敬，而心孚
translation_en:
…the flood, there was Yu to bring the waters and land into order; for teaching sowing and harvesting, there was Ji to provide grain for the multitude; for clarifying punishments, there was Gao Yao to support moral instruction. In assisting the rulers’ actions and lending discernment to their hearing, each fulfilled his duties when their rule stood at its zenith. Wherever government remained imperfect, virtue unrectified, or the use of resources unbeneficial, the ministers of that time brought the work to completion on their rulers’ behalf. Thus Yao and Shun enjoyed the ease of governing without action: harmony prevailed, and their transforming influence spread like the wind. Among the supreme achievements of government celebrated past and present, those of Tang and Yu remain unsurpassed.
Among worthy kings, none surpassed King Xuan of Zhou, who indeed accomplished a restoration of his dynasty. At its outset, the Huaiyi rebelled, and he thought of chastising them; the Jingman became enemies, and he thought of campaigning against them; the Xianyun showed no restraint, and he thought of attacking them. Yet King Xuan likewise never had to toil himself. Reciting the Book of Odes and reading such poems as “Gathering Bracken,” we find that, for pacifying the Huaiyi, there was the Earl of Shao, who traveled about proclaiming the royal commands; for campaigning against the Jingman, there was the venerable elder Fang Shu; for attacking the Xianyun, there was Ji Fu, accomplished in both civil and military affairs. In hastening to service and warding off aggression, each displayed his abilities in those troubled times. Wherever royal military levies had not been furnished, chariots and troops were not at full strength, or overall administration remained incomplete, the ministers of that time all discharged their responsibilities. Thus King Xuan enjoyed orderly government without personal toil, with the realm well governed and royal authority held in awe. Among the dynastic restorations celebrated past and present, that of Zhou remains difficult to equal.
From that time onward, without ministers who assisted their rulers’ actions and lent discernment to their hearing, how could anyone hope for government equal in splendor to that of the Two Emperors? Without ministers who hastened to service and warded off aggression, how could anyone hope for government surpassing the excellence of the Zhou king? It is fitting that Your Majesty should praise and admire them, and regard the ages after the Three Dynasties as too inferior to merit discussion. Your Majesty deepens the reverence of your pure sacrifices, and your heart finds accord with…

穹昊茂熈洽之化而光紹
祖宗以言其安内也
内苑耕籍重稼穡之艱難
殿工擬竣蠲各省之徵派憂下民之易虐則申
嚴考察之令慮犯法之無知則時重恤刑之
典發倉廪以賑民乏施藥餌以療民痾其恩
澤之溥及於遐邇者不啻如雲雨之行施沛
乎沾濡而無物之弗被矣以言其攘外也内
立三營開戎府以固京師之本外重九邊慎
將帥以嚴疆場之防醜虜内侵則
===
神謨密運即以驅逐于塞漠島夷外寇則
天威奮迅即以勦截於海濱意出而鬼神率從令
行而姦宄懾伏其威武之震疊於邊陲者不
啻如雷霆之鼓舞肅乎烜耀而無遠之不服
矣
身居九重而慮周四海之外
尊臨五位而威制八荒之遐天下臣民方仰協和
風動順治威嚴之治軼唐虞而越有周矣夫
何邇年以来旱潦頻仍而倉箱無卒歳之儲
公私俱困而杼軸有其空之患北虜乗飈舉

穹昊，茂熈洽之化，而光紹祖宗。以言其安内也，内苑耕籍，重稼穡之艱難；殿工擬竣，蠲各省之徵派。憂下民之易虐，則申嚴考察之令；慮犯法之無知，則時重恤刑之典。發倉廪以賑民乏，施藥餌以療民痾。其恩澤之溥及於遐邇者，不啻如雲雨之行施，沛乎沾濡，而無物之弗被矣。以言其攘外也，内立三營，開戎府，以固京師之本；外重九邊，慎將帥，以嚴疆場之防。醜虜内侵，則神謨密運，即以驅逐于塞漠；島夷外寇，則天威奮迅，即以勦截於海濱。意出而鬼神率從，令行而姦宄懾伏。其威武之震疊於邊陲者，不啻如雷霆之鼓舞，肅乎烜耀，而無遠之不服矣。身居九重，而慮周四海之外；尊臨五位，而威制八荒之遐。天下臣民方仰協和風動、順治威嚴之治，軼唐虞而越有周矣。

夫何邇年以来，旱潦頻仍，而倉箱無卒歳之儲；公私俱困，而杼軸有其空之患；北虜乗飈舉
translation_en:
…vast Heaven; you foster flourishing harmony through your transforming influence and gloriously carry on the legacy of your ancestors. As for securing peace within, you personally plough the ritual field in the inner imperial park, recognizing the hardships of sowing and reaping. With work on the palace halls approaching completion, you remit the levies imposed on the various provinces. Concerned that the common people may readily suffer oppression, you reiterate strict orders for the evaluations of officials. Fearing that people may break the law through ignorance, you repeatedly emphasize the provisions for compassion in administering punishments. You open the granaries to relieve the people's want and distribute medicines to cure their illnesses. Your beneficence reaches far and near like clouds dispensing rain, abundantly soaking all things and leaving none untouched.

As for repelling external threats, within you establish the Three Training Divisions and set up military headquarters to strengthen the foundations of the capital; beyond, you give weight to the Nine Frontier Commands and exercise care in choosing commanders, making the frontier defenses formidable. When the odious northern foes invade, your divine plans operate in secret, promptly driving them out to the frontier deserts. When the island barbarians raid from abroad, your heavenly might springs swiftly into action, promptly exterminating and intercepting them along the coast. When your intention is expressed, spirits and gods all obey; when your commands are put into effect, evildoers cower in submission. Your martial might shakes the borderlands like the stirring force of thunder, awesome and radiant, leaving no place so distant that it does not submit. Though you dwell within the ninefold palace, your care encompasses lands beyond the Four Seas; occupying the exalted fifth position of sovereignty, your might controls even the distant Eight Wastes. All the officials and people of the realm now look up to your rule: its harmonizing influence moves them like the wind, and its orderly government inspires awe. It surpasses the ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun and exceeds even the Zhou.

Why, then, in recent years have droughts and floods repeatedly occurred, leaving granaries and grain bins without stores sufficient to last the year? Why are public and private resources alike exhausted, with the people's looms standing empty? The northern foes ride the force of a rising whirlwind…

之勢而不時擾我邊鄙南賊鼓烏集之羣而
連歲犯我海壖誠如
聖制所謂水旱爲災黎民阻饑戎狄白警南賊尤
甚有以厪
宵旰之懷矣臣以爲天地之大也不能必寒暑災
祥之正堯舜之聖也猶且病博施濟衆之難

…necessarily be diligent in nurturing the people. Those who speak of fitting punishments do not necessarily understand the way of moral instruction. Some reputed to be scrupulously upright [?] force themselves to act so in pursuit of praise, yet cannot remain constant to the end; some called benevolent rulers dispense petty kindnesses to purchase favor, yet remain blind to greater concerns. Worse still, some oppress the people to enrich themselves and injure them to gratify their own desires. The people fear only that these men will not leave. How can one expect them to rescue the people from hardship, relieve their suffering, and carry out the sovereign’s commands for their benefit? Among those sent forth with chariots and battle-axes and entrusted with armies, there is no lack of generals. Yet those serving among the royal guards do not necessarily possess the equipment for martial prowess; those bearing the name of the realm’s shield and rampart do not necessarily excel at strategy devised over ceremonial vessels. Those enjoying great prestige throughout the realm still embellish hollow reputations to claim credit; those entrusted with supreme authority beyond the capital still indulge in brutality that harms their men. Men who wielded butchers’ knives or guarded gates display a spirit that would overawe the armies, yet one never hears of their personally braving arrows and stones to win even a single day’s victory. Sons of privilege clad in fine silks, whose families have worn sable tails and gold ornaments for generations, merely read their fathers’ military books and obscure the achievements of successive generations. Worse still, commanders-in-chief fear their subordinate generals, and subordinate generals fear their soldiers: there is no limit to what may ensue. 而寇患以除民安而邦本以固災咎可弭困窮
可復以媲美虞周之治其何道而可臣愚以為
吏有之今之郡守民之師帥也所當重也是
必嚴考覈之典申久任之規循良悃愊者增
秩以示榮久之若卓茂之封而不以為驟闒
茸貪墨者重罰以示辱甚則若阿大夫之烹
而不以為苛然後甄別殿最之典明吏將砥
礪以自勉而撫字之陽城寬和之黃霸自輩
出矣而以是牧民民困其少蘇乎志有之將
者國之輔也所當重也是必專委任之柄隆
===
駕馭之權有功必賞不間於羣言如任樂羊
而無有於二志有罪必懲不牽於私故如戮
馬謖而罔萌夫貸心然後鼓舞振作之用行
將皆激昻以求試而良平之督撫韓白之統
率自羣起矣而以是除盜盜患其少息乎如
是則得文臣以宣惠惠無不浹而國家之元
氣自固足以安內而紓鴻鴈之憂得武將以
揚威威無不奮而國家之神氣自振足以攘
外而免墉隼之害
陛下可端冕服而神不顯之德可寧黼扆而成顒

Those who govern conscientiously and with sincere devotion should receive increases in rank to mark their distinction; in time, they might even be enfeoffed as Zhuo Mao was, without this being regarded as precipitous promotion. The base, incompetent, and corrupt should receive heavy punishments to mark their disgrace; in extreme cases, they might even be boiled to death like the Grand Master of A, without this being regarded as excessive severity. Only then will the rules for distinguishing the worst from the best in performance be made clear. Officials will strive to improve themselves, and men like Yang Cheng, who nurtured the people, and Huang Ba, who governed with generosity and harmony, will arise in succession. With such men shepherding the people, might the people’s distress not be somewhat relieved?

Merit must invariably be rewarded, without allowing the voices of the multitude to sow discord—as when Yue Yang was entrusted with command, with no wavering of purpose. Offenses must invariably be punished, without being swayed by personal ties—as when Ma Su was executed, without any thought of granting him clemency. Only then will measures to inspire and invigorate them take effect. Generals will all eagerly seek opportunities to prove themselves, and supreme commanders and grand coordinators like Zhang Liang and Chen Ping, and military commanders like Han Xin and Bai Qi, will arise in numbers. With such men eliminating bandits, might the scourge of banditry not somewhat abate?

text:
若之孚正猶天道默運於上而四時之官五
行之吏各効其職以生萬物而萬物羣然其
樂生焉怡然其並育焉二帝無為之治於此
復覩而周宣中興之業可以駕而上之矣然
所謂任吏擇將又豈無其要哉今之吏治不
得其人非吏之果無良也亦曰學校之教不
明耳學校者守令自出之地也今之學校臣
惑焉涉經傳以組詞章者曰足以取青紫裂
章句以飾文藝者曰足以致顯榮而於身心
道德之懿漫不之知及出而從政則仗逢迎
===
為捷徑視職署為置郵無異乎文職之不修
也為今之計當思所以重其教若三物之規
九經之訓倣古而行之以端其趨向則菁莪
樂育之教興而濟濟之多士為王國之楨矣
今之將領不得其人非將之真不才也亦曰
武舉之科不嚴耳武舉者將才發軔之地也
今之武舉臣惑焉繇弓矢得者皆挽強之粗
才以策論進者惟蹈襲之舊語而於韜畧奇
正之實漫不之究及出而行師則鉛刀不足
以為割朽壤不足以為障無怪乎武功之不

若之孚，正猶天道默運於上，而四時之官、五行之吏各効其職，以生萬物，而萬物羣然其樂生焉，怡然其並育焉。二帝無為之治於此復覩，而周宣中興之業可以駕而上之矣。然所謂任吏擇將，又豈無其要哉？
今之吏治不得其人，非吏之果無良也，亦曰學校之教不明耳。學校者，守令自出之地也。今之學校，臣惑焉。涉經傳以組詞章者，曰足以取青紫；裂章句以飾文藝者，曰足以致顯榮。而於身心道德之懿，漫不之知。及出而從政，則仗逢迎為捷徑，視職署為置郵，無異乎文職之不修也。為今之計，當思所以重其教。若三物之規、九經之訓，倣古而行之，以端其趨向，則菁莪樂育之教興，而濟濟之多士為王國之楨矣。
今之將領不得其人，非將之真不才也，亦曰武舉之科不嚴耳。武舉者，將才發軔之地也。今之武舉，臣惑焉。繇弓矢得者，皆挽強之粗才；以策論進者，惟蹈襲之舊語。而於韜畧奇正之實，漫不之究。及出而行師，則鉛刀不足以為割，朽壤不足以為障，無怪乎武功之不
translation_en:
…such reverent trust. This would be just like the Way of Heaven silently operating above, while the officers of the four seasons and the functionaries of the five phases each fulfill their duties to bring forth the myriad things. All things together would delight in living and flourish contentedly side by side. The government through nonaction of the Two Emperors, Yao and Shun, would be seen again here, and the achievement of King Xuan of Zhou in restoring his dynasty could be surpassed. Yet surely there are also essential principles for what is called appointing officials and selecting generals?
That civil administration today does not obtain the right men is not because officials truly lack good qualities; it is simply that instruction in the schools is not clearly established. The schools are where prefects and magistrates originate. Your servant is perplexed by the schools of today. Those who skim the classics and commentaries to weave literary compositions say that this suffices to obtain the blue and purple insignia of office; those who tear apart chapters and sentences to embellish their writing say that this suffices to attain distinction and glory. Yet they know nothing of the excellence of personal cultivation and moral virtue. When they emerge to enter government service, they rely on ingratiation as a shortcut and regard their offices as relay stations. This amounts to neglect of civil duties [?]. What must now be considered is how to give greater weight to their instruction. Such models as the three subjects of instruction and the teachings of the nine guiding principles should be put into practice in imitation of antiquity, to set their aspirations straight. Then the education that delights in nurturing talent, celebrated in “Luxuriant Southernwood,” will flourish, and the abundant company of worthy men will become pillars of the royal realm.
That military commands today do not obtain the right men is not because generals truly lack ability; it is simply that the military examination is insufficiently rigorous. The military examination is where men of military talent begin their careers. Your servant is perplexed by the military examinations of today. Those selected through archery are all men of crude ability who can draw powerful bows; those advanced through policy essays and discourses merely repeat stale phrases. Yet they make no inquiry into the substance of military strategy or the use of unorthodox and orthodox tactics. When they go out to lead armies, they are like leaden knives incapable of cutting and crumbling earth incapable of forming a defensive barrier. No wonder military achievement fails to…

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
競也爲今之計當思所以慎其科若大射之
禮大閱之法倣古而行之以新其志意則兎
罝好仇之化成而赳赳之武夫爲公侯之腹
心矣由是文武將吏各得其人又何患惠澤
不宣而旱潦之爲災威強不振而虜寇之足
虞哉雖然運操縱之大機用磨礪之大法則
尤有大本焉宋儒程頤曰朝廷者監司之本
監司者守令之綱也欲使民之得其所本原
之地亦在乎朝廷而已朱熹曰聖王所以制
禦蠻夷之道其本不在威強而在德業其具
===
===
不在兵食而在紀綱其備不在邊境而在朝
廷而朝廷之要則漢儒董仲舒曰人君正心
以正朝廷正朝廷以正百官正百官以正萬
民而已蓋人君一心取人立政之本也今
陛下敬一持心無逸示訓而凡取人立政者取諸
一心而有餘矣而臣今日欲效忠於
陛下者非外此而有加也惟在常存敬一無逸之
心而涵泳之耳伏願
陛下法天行之健繼離照之明緝之爲不息之誠
衍之爲無疆之業端養於清穆之表則防未

punctuated: 競也。爲今之計，當思所以慎其科。若大射之禮、大閱之法，倣古而行之，以新其志意，則兎罝好仇之化成，而赳赳之武夫爲公侯之腹心矣。由是文武將吏各得其人，又何患惠澤不宣而旱潦之爲災，威強不振而虜寇之足虞哉？雖然，運操縱之大機，用磨礪之大法，則尤有大本焉。宋儒程頤曰：「朝廷者，監司之本；監司者，守令之綱也。欲使民之得其所，本原之地亦在乎朝廷而已。」朱熹曰：「聖王所以制禦蠻夷之道，其本不在威強而在德業，其具不在兵食而在紀綱，其備不在邊境而在朝廷。」而朝廷之要，則漢儒董仲舒曰：「人君正心以正朝廷，正朝廷以正百官，正百官以正萬民。」而已。蓋人君一心，取人立政之本也。今陛下敬一持心，無逸示訓，而凡取人立政者，取諸一心而有餘矣。而臣今日欲效忠於陛下者，非外此而有加也，惟在常存敬一無逸之心而涵泳之耳。伏願陛下法天行之健，繼離照之明，緝之爲不息之誠，衍之爲無疆之業，端養於清穆之表，則防未
translation_en:
…fail to flourish. The course to take now is to consider how to conduct the military examination with due care. If the rites of the Great Archery Ceremony and the procedures of the Grand Military Review were carried out in imitation of antiquity, renewing the candidates’ aspirations, then the transforming influence celebrated in “Rabbit Nets,” with its “worthy companions,” would be realized, and valiant warriors would become the trusted confidants of dukes and lords. With suitable men thus secured as civil and military officials and commanders, why need we fear that beneficence would fail to reach the people and droughts and floods become disasters, or that military might would fail to assert itself and foreign foes and bandits give cause for alarm?
Nevertheless, wielding the great mechanism of control and applying the great methods of honing men’s abilities depend above all on a fundamental foundation. The Song Confucian Cheng Yi said: “The imperial court is the foundation of the surveillance commissioners; the surveillance commissioners are the guiding framework for prefects and county magistrates. If one wishes the people to find their proper place, the ultimate source lies solely in the imperial court.” Zhu Xi said: “In the sage kings’ way of controlling the barbarians, the foundation lies in virtuous achievement, not military might; the means lie in institutional order, not troops and provisions; and the defenses lie in the imperial court, not the frontier.” As for what is essential to the imperial court, it is simply what the Han Confucian Dong Zhongshu said: “The ruler rectifies his heart in order to rectify the imperial court; he rectifies the imperial court in order to rectify the hundred officials; and he rectifies the hundred officials in order to rectify the myriad people.”
The ruler’s own heart is indeed the foundation for selecting men and establishing government. Now Your Majesty governs your heart through reverent single-mindedness and offers instruction through “Against Ease.” For everything involved in selecting men and establishing government, the resources of this one heart are more than sufficient. In seeking today to serve Your Majesty loyally, your servant has nothing to add beyond this: only that you constantly preserve a heart of reverent single-mindedness, free from indulgence in ease, and steep yourself in these principles.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will emulate the vigor of Heaven’s movement and perpetuate the brightness of Li, the trigram of illumination; sustain this as unceasing sincerity and extend it into an achievement without bounds. By upright cultivation amid an outward bearing of serene dignity, you will guard against what has not yet …

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
萌之欲而於好惡無所偏矯易溺之情而於
愛憎無所徇也獨斷於臨蒞之際則兼天下
之聰明以為智而於視聽無所壅順天下之
心志以施令而於取舍無所私也由是心不
待檢而自存可以游神於至道之域而德日
益純志不假持而自固可以澄心於湛一之
天而業日益弘如日月之久照而不改其明
如四時之久成而不愆其紀如天地之久運
而不息其機以此取人人無不得以此立政
政無不舉而中外臣工罔不惕厲以共厥職
===
文恬武煕之績以奏內安外攘之效以臻至
道成和平之美
國祚衍靈長之慶誠可遠追二帝雍煕之化近
軼周王嘉靖之休即軒皇久道華胥之治不
外是矣臣愚幸甚天下幸甚臣無任戰悚隕
越之至臣謹對

如四時之久成而不忒其紀如天地之久運
而不息其機以此取人人無不得以此立政
政無不舉而中外臣工罔不惕厲以共厥職
===
文恬武熈〔一一〕績以奏内安外攘之效以臻至
道成和平之美
國祚衍靈長之慶誠可遠追二帝雍熈之化近
軼周王嘉靖之休即軒皇久道華胥之治不
外是矣臣愚幸甚天下幸甚臣無任戰悚隕
越之至臣謹對
punctuated: 萌之欲，而於好惡無所偏；矯易溺之情，而於愛憎無所徇也。獨斷於臨蒞之際，則兼天下之聰明以為智，而於視聽無所壅；順天下之心志以施令，而於取舍無所私也。由是，心不待檢而自存，可以游神於至道之域，而德日益純；志不假持而自固，可以澄心於湛一之天，而業日益弘。如日月之久照而不改其明，如四時之久成而不愆其紀，如天地之久運而不息其機。以此取人，人無不得；以此立政，政無不舉。而中外臣工罔不惕厲以共厥職，文恬武煕之績以奏，內安外攘之效以臻，至道成和平之美，國祚衍靈長之慶。誠可遠追二帝雍煕之化，近軼周王嘉靖之休，即軒皇久道華胥之治，不外是矣。臣愚幸甚，天下幸甚。臣無任戰悚隕越之至，臣謹對。
translation_en:
…desires before they sprout, so that likes and dislikes are free of partiality; correct feelings that readily succumb to indulgence, so that affection and aversion do not lead to favoritism. When exercising sole judgment in governing, draw upon the keen hearing and clear sight of all under Heaven to inform your wisdom, so that nothing obstructs what you see and hear; issue commands in accord with the hearts and aspirations of all under Heaven, so that your choices and rejections are free of selfishness. Thus the mind will preserve itself without requiring restraint, allowing your spirit to roam in the realm of the highest Way, while your virtue grows purer each day. Your resolve will remain firm without requiring support, allowing your mind to become clear in a heaven of tranquil unity, while your achievements grow greater each day. Like the sun and moon, which shine enduringly without diminishing their brightness; like the four seasons, which continually bring things to completion without departing from their order; like Heaven and Earth, which revolve enduringly without their workings ceasing: with this, select men, and every appointment will find the right person; with this, establish government, and every undertaking will be accomplished. All officials at court and beyond will diligently and vigilantly discharge their duties. The accomplishments of civil tranquility and military flourishing will be achieved, and the effects of peace within and the repulsion of threats from without will be attained. Through the highest Way, the beauty of harmony and peace will be realized, and the dynasty’s allotted span will be extended in blessed longevity.

Truly, this could emulate the harmonious and flourishing transformation wrought by the Two Emperors of remote antiquity, and surpass the blessings of the Zhou kings’ admirable and tranquil rule in more recent times. Even Emperor Xuanyuan’s enduring Way and the governance of Huaxu amount to no more than this. Your foolish servant would be most fortunate, and all under Heaven most fortunate. Your servant is overcome with trembling apprehension and the utmost fear of stumbling and failing. Your servant respectfully submits this reply.

translation_en:
Sequence of Imperial Honors

On the morning of the fifteenth day of the third month in the forty-first year of Jiajing (1562), the tribute scholars proceeded to the inner palace for the Palace Examination. The Emperor took his seat at the Dachao Gate and personally bestowed the policy questions.

On the morning of the eighteenth day of the third month, all civil and military officials attended in their court robes, standing in their assigned ranks. That day, the Embroidered Uniform Guard arrayed the ceremonial regalia within the vermilion courtyard. The Emperor took his seat at the Dachao Gate, and officials of the Court of State Ceremonial transmitted the imperial decree and called out the successful candidates’ names. Officials of the Ministry of Rites carried the yellow announcement, led by drums and music, out beyond the Chang’an Left Gate. After it had been posted, officials of Shuntian Prefecture escorted the first-place graduate back to his residence with parasols, canopies, and a ceremonial retinue.

On the nineteenth day of the third month…

translation_en:
Second Class: eighty-five men, granted the status of metropolitan graduate (jinshi).

Qi Yuanzuo 戚元佐 was registered in an artisan household in Jiaxing County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang. An Imperial University student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he had the courtesy name Xizhong and ranked fourth in his family. He was thirty-three sui, born on the sixteenth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Fu, his grandfather Ze, his father Shan, and his mother Lady Zhang. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Yuanzai, Yuanfu (a metropolitan graduate), and Yuanbi. He married Lady Lü. He placed twenty-second in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 265th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xiang Ke 項鈳 was registered in a civilian household in Jiashan County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, and was a native of Jiaxing County. A county government student specializing in the Book of Documents, he had the courtesy name Bingrong and ranked first in his family. He was thirty-four sui, born on the twentieth day of the fifth month. His great-grandfather Heng was posthumously awarded the title of Left Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate. His grandfather Zhong was Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent and Minister of War, with the posthumous name Xiangyi. His father was Ji and his mother Lady Sheng; both parents were living. His elder brothers were Yong (Vice Commander), Kai (Usher), Tang (Battalion Commander), Zhen (an Imperial University student), Xi (Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments in Nanjing), Jinfeng, Yinfeng, and Kuang. He married Lady Shen. He placed eighth in both the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and the Metropolitan Examination.

Pan Yunduan 潘允端 was registered in a civilian household in Shanghai County, Songjiang Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Rites, he had the courtesy name Zhonglü and ranked second in his family. He was thirty-seven sui, born on the fourteenth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather Qing was posthumously awarded the title of Left Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate. His grandfather Kui was Assistant Surveillance Commissioner in Sichuan and was posthumously awarded the title of Left Censor-in-Chief. His father En was Left Censor-in-Chief. His father's former wife, Lady Bao, was posthumously granted the title of Lady; his mother, Lady Cao, was granted the same title. Both his father and mother were living. His elder brother was Yunzhe (a Metropolitan Examination graduate awaiting the Palace Examination). His younger brothers were Yunzhen, Yunxiu (an Imperial University student), Yunliang (Recorder in the Court of Imperial Entertainments), Yunzang, Yunzheng, Yunda (an Imperial University student), Yungao, Yunzhong, Yungong, Yunfu, and Yunji. He married Lady Gu. He placed fifth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 211th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
First Class: three men, granted the distinction of metropolitan graduate with honors (jinshi jidi).

Xu Shixing, registered in a civilian household in Wu County, Suzhou Prefecture, Directly Administered Region, was a native of Changzhou County and a county school student. He specialized in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Rumo; he ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-six years old, born on the sixteenth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zhou, his grandfather Qian, and his father Shizhang; his mother was née Wang and his stepmother née Huang. His grandparents and parents were living. His younger brothers were Shide, Shihua, and Shijie; his wife was née Wu. He placed third in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and twenty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Xijue, registered in a civilian household in Taicang Subprefecture, Suzhou Prefecture, Directly Administered Region, was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals. His courtesy name was Yuanyu; he ranked first among his brothers and was twenty-nine years old, born on the twenty-first day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Shen, his grandfather Yong, and his father Mengxiang, a student of the Directorate of Education; his mother was née Wu. Both parents were living. His younger brother Dingjue was a student of the Directorate of Education; his wife was née Zhu. He placed fourth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yu Youding, registered in a civilian household in Yin County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a student of the Directorate of Education. He specialized in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Bingzhong; he ranked second among his brothers and was thirty-six years old, born on the eighteenth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather Tang and grandfather Huang both held honorary official titles for longevity; his father Yonglin was an Assistant Prefect. His mother was née Wang. Both parents were deceased. His elder brother was Youren; his wife was née Shui. He placed fifty-fourth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Li Cai, registered in Fengcheng County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, belonged to a military household and was an added-quota student at the prefectural school. He specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals; his courtesy name was Mengcheng. Sixth in birth order, he was aged thirty-four and born on the seventeenth day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Yuhao; his grandfather, Wanping, was granted the title of Bureau Director in the Ministry of Justice; and his father, Sui, was Minister of War at Nanjing. His mother, née Lai, was ennobled as Lady of Suitability, and his stepmother, née Yan, as Lady of Respect. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Shu, a tribute student; Ge, an Assistant Commander; Hang, a tribute student; Su, a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the same examination cohort; and Shi, who had passed the Metropolitan Examination (gongshi). His younger brothers were Nan, an Imperial University student; Chan, a county school student; and Zhen. He married a woman née Yuan and subsequently a woman née Tu. He placed ninth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and sixty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Junmin, registered in Puzhou, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, belonged to a civilian household and was an Imperial University student. He specialized in the Book of Rites; his courtesy name was Bozhang. First in birth order, he was aged thirty-two and born on the thirtieth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather, Xuan, was posthumously granted the titles of Grand Master of Glorious Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Guardian concurrently serving as Grand Preceptor of the Heir Apparent, and Minister of War. His grandfather, Zhan, was Assistant Surveillance Commissioner in Sichuan and received the same titles posthumously. His father, Bo, held those titles and offices. His mother, née Duan, was ennobled as a Lady of the First Rank. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Junshi and Junyan, students admitted by virtue of family office; Junqing, a regular Battalion Commander in the Embroidered-Uniform Guard; and Junchen. He married a woman née Shi. He placed fortieth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Fu Lin, registered in Xinzhou, Taiyuan Prefecture, Shanxi, belonged to a civilian household and was an Imperial University student. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Yingqi. First in birth order, he was aged thirty-one and born on the twenty-ninth day of the first month. His great-grandfather, Tianxi, was a Professor; his grandfather, Kang, was an Imperial University student; and his father, Chaoxuan, was a Ceremonial Escort, a husband of an imperial clanswoman. His legal mother was the Township Lady of Langqing, and his birth mother was née Yin. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Zhen, who had passed the Metropolitan Examination (gongshi), Pei, and Ni. He married a woman née Zhao. He placed twenty-first in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and two hundred fiftieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Shan, registered in Longxi County, Zhangzhou Prefecture, Fujian, belonged to a civilian household and was a county school student. He specialized in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Yuanfu. Third in birth order, he was aged thirty-one and born on the twenty-second day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Dinong; his grandfather, Ruizhe; his father, Zhangyu; and his mother, née Xu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Shen and his younger brother was Dai. He married a woman née Kang. He placed thirty-second in the Fujian Provincial Examination and one hundred twenty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
萬廷言〔貫江西南昌府南昌縣民籍府學生治詩經字曰忠行四年三十三十二月初九日生〕
曾祖必昌祖廣載〔封知縣〕父虞愷〔總督南京糧儲都察院右副都御史〕母蕭氏〔封孺人〕
重慶下弟廷藎廷餼廷贊廷試廷寅廷安廷宣娶鄒氏
江西鄉試第二名會試第二百三十五名
徐用檢〔貫浙江金華府蘭谿縣民籍國子生治易經字克賢行三十二年三十五十月十三日生〕
曾祖芝祖講父締嫡母章氏生母楊氏
慈侍下兄用圭用光〔工部郎中〕弟用乾用脩用襄用威用齊用登用辟娶鄭氏
浙江鄉試第三十三名會試第一百三十四名
===
王宜〔貫福建興化府莆田縣民籍縣學附學生治詩經字時行行二年三十四月初二日生〕
曾祖元二祖巨甫父絹〔知縣〕母殳氏
重慶下兄佐弟偉俊傑賓宦寀宇娶陸氏
福建鄉試第五十五名會試第二百四十七名
葉以蕃〔貫浙江處州府遂昌縣民籍國子生治詩經字承叔行二十六年二十七十二月十六日生〕
曾祖昭祖魁父弘淵母王氏
具慶下兄以弁以芬以芳弟以峯以蓁娶黃氏
順天府鄉試第五十二名會試第十九名

慈侍下 兄用圭 用光〔工部郎中〕 弟用乾 用修 用襄 用威 用晉 用登 用辭 娶鄭氏
浙江鄉試第三十三名 會試第一百三十四名
===
王宜 貫福建興化府莆田縣民籍 縣學附學生
治詩經字時行行二年三十四月初二日生
曾祖元二 祖巨甫 父緝〔知縣〕 母史氏
重慶下 兄佐 弟偉 俊 傑 賓 宦 家 宇 娶陸氏
福建鄉試第五十五名 會試第二百四十七名
葉以蕃 貫浙江處州府遂昌縣民籍 國子生
治詩經字承叔行二十六年二十七十二月十六日生
曾祖昭 祖魁 父弘淵 母王氏
具慶下 兄以并 以芬 以芳 弟以華 以蓁 娶黃氏
順天府鄉試第五十二名 會試第十九名
punctuated:
萬廷言〔貫江西南昌府南昌縣，民籍，府學生，治《詩經》，字曰忠，行四，年三十三，十二月初九日生〕。曾祖必昌，祖廣載〔封知縣〕，父虞愷〔總督南京糧儲都察院右副都御史〕，母蕭氏〔封孺人〕。重慶下，弟廷藎、廷餼、廷贊、廷試、廷寅、廷安、廷宣，娶鄒氏。江西鄉試第二名，會試第二百三十五名。

徐用檢〔貫浙江金華府蘭谿縣，民籍，國子生，治《易經》，字克賢，行三十二，年三十五，十月十三日生〕。曾祖芝，祖講，父締，嫡母章氏，生母楊氏。慈侍下，兄用圭、用光〔工部郎中〕，弟用乾、用脩、用襄、用威、用齊、用登、用辟，娶鄭氏。浙江鄉試第三十三名，會試第一百三十四名。

王宜〔貫福建興化府莆田縣，民籍，縣學附學生，治《詩經》，字時行，行二，年三十，四月初二日生〕。曾祖元二，祖巨甫，父絹〔知縣〕，母殳氏。重慶下，兄佐，弟偉、俊、傑、賓、宦、寀、宇，娶陸氏。福建鄉試第五十五名，會試第二百四十七名。

葉以蕃〔貫浙江處州府遂昌縣，民籍，國子生，治《詩經》，字承叔，行二十六，年二十七，十二月十六日生〕。曾祖昭，祖魁，父弘淵，母王氏。具慶下，兄以弁、以芬、以芳，弟以峯、以蓁，娶黃氏。順天府鄉試第五十二名，會試第十九名。
translation_en:
Wan Tingyan, of Nanchang County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, was registered in a civilian household and was a prefectural school student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Yuezhong; he ranked fourth in his family and was thirty-three years old, born on the ninth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Bichang; his grandfather, Guangzai, received the honorary title of District Magistrate; his father, Yukai, was Right Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate, serving as Superintendent of Grain Storage at Nanjing; and his mother, née Xiao, received the title of Lady (ruren). His grandparents and parents were living. His younger brothers were Tingjin, Tingxi, Tingzan, Tingshi, Tingyin, Ting’an, and Tingxuan, and his wife was née Zou. He placed second in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 235th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Yongjian, of Lanxi County, Jinhua Prefecture, Zhejiang, was registered in a civilian household and was a Directorate of Education student specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Kexian; he ranked thirty-second in his family and was thirty-five years old, born on the thirteenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Zhi; his grandfather, Jiang; and his father, Di. His legal mother was née Zhang, and his birth mother was née Yang. His father was deceased, and his mother was living. His elder brothers were Yonggui and Yongguang, the latter a Bureau Director in the Ministry of Works; his younger brothers were Yongqian, Yongxiu, Yongxiang, Yongwei, Yongqi, Yongdeng, and Yongbi. His wife was née Zheng. He placed thirty-third in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 134th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Yi, of Putian County, Xinghua Prefecture, Fujian, was registered in a civilian household and was an attached student of the county school specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Shixing; he ranked second in his family and was thirty years old, born on the second day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Yuan’er; his grandfather, Jufu; his father, Juan, a District Magistrate; and his mother, née Shu. His grandparents and parents were living. His elder brother was Zuo, and his younger brothers were Wei, Jun, Jie, Bin, Huan, Cai, and Yu. His wife was née Lu. He placed fifty-fifth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 247th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ye Yifan, of Suichang County, Chuzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was registered in a civilian household and was a Directorate of Education student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Chengshu; he ranked twenty-sixth in his family and was twenty-seven years old, born on the sixteenth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Zhao; his grandfather, Kui; his father, Hongyuan; and his mother, née Wang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Yibian, Yifen, and Yifang, and his younger brothers were Yifeng and Yizhen. His wife was née Huang. He placed fifty-second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and nineteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
徐元氣〔貫直隸寧國府宣城縣儒籍國子生治易經字汝和行二年三十十月初七日生〕
曾祖愈〔歲貢生〕祖訪〔典膳〕父衢〔縣主簿〕母劉氏
具慶下兄元策〔貢士〕弟元期元霸元祥元選元太元亨元祉元訂元愷元禎元禮元祝娶張氏
應天府鄉試第三十名會試第三十一名
陳大章〔貫浙江寧波府鄞縣民籍縣學生治詩經字祖堯行三十六年三十一五月十五日生〕
曾祖勲〔府經歷〕祖□〔□□〕父藩前母董氏母柴氏
具慶下弟大韶大夏娶伍氏
浙江鄉試第十七名會試第七十八名
===
闕繼禹〔貫四川敘州府南溪縣民籍國子生治詩經字叔敬行一年三十四月初四日生〕
曾祖爵〔縣丞〕祖守萬父濟母楊氏
具慶下兄時泰弟師禹娶帥氏
四川鄉試第六十四名會試第二百六十名
鍾振〔貫廣東廉州府合浦縣民籍歲貢生治詩經字玉甫行一年三十一正月初二日生〕
曾祖黙祖信父文母李氏
具慶下弟揚撰掄捷娶劉氏
順天府鄉試第二十五名會試第五十七名

徐元氣貫直隷寧國府宣城縣儒籍　國子生

治詩經字粹□行三十六年三十一五月十五日生
曾祖懃〔府經歷〕　祖□〔□□〕　父潘　前母董氏　母柴氏
具慶下　弟大部　大夏　娶伍氏
浙江鄉試第十七名　會試第七十八名
===
闞繼禹貫四川敘州府南溪縣民籍　國子生
治詩經字叔敘行一年三十四月初四日生
曾祖爵〔縣主簿〕　祖守萬　父濟　母楊氏
具慶下　兄時泰　弟師禹　娶師氏
四川鄉試第六十四名　會試第二百六十名
鍾振貫廣東廉州府合浦縣民籍　歲貢生
治詩經字玉甫行一年三十一正月初二日生
曾祖黙　祖信　父文　母李氏
具慶下　弟揚　撰　掄　捷　娶劉氏
順天府鄉試第二十五名　會試第五十七名
punctuated:
徐元氣〔貫直隸寧國府宣城縣，儒籍，國子生，治易經，字汝和，行二，年三十，十月初七日生〕。曾祖愈〔歲貢生〕，祖訪〔典膳〕，父衢〔縣主簿〕，母劉氏。具慶下，兄元策〔貢士〕，弟元期、元霸、元祥、元選、元太、元亨、元祉、元訂、元愷、元禎、元禮、元祝，娶張氏。應天府鄉試第三十名，會試第三十一名。

陳大章〔貫浙江寧波府鄞縣，民籍，縣學生，治詩經，字祖堯，行三十六，年三十一，五月十五日生〕。曾祖勲〔府經歷〕，祖□〔□□〕，父藩，前母董氏，母柴氏。具慶下，弟大韶、大夏，娶伍氏。浙江鄉試第十七名，會試第七十八名。

闕繼禹〔貫四川敘州府南溪縣，民籍，國子生，治詩經，字叔敬，行一，年三十，四月初四日生〕。曾祖爵〔縣丞〕，祖守萬，父濟，母楊氏。具慶下，兄時泰，弟師禹，娶帥氏。四川鄉試第六十四名，會試第二百六十名。

鍾振〔貫廣東廉州府合浦縣，民籍，歲貢生，治詩經，字玉甫，行一，年三十一，正月初二日生〕。曾祖黙，祖信，父文，母李氏。具慶下，弟揚、撰、掄、捷，娶劉氏。順天府鄉試第二十五名，會試第五十七名。
translation_en:
Xu Yuanqi, registered in Xuancheng County, Ningguo Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region (Zhili), belonged to a scholar household and was an Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Changes. His courtesy name was Ruhe; he ranked second in his family and was aged thirty, born on the seventh day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yu, an annual tribute student; his grandfather was Fang, a Steward; his father was Qu, a County Registrar; and his mother was née Liu. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Yuance, a tribute scholar (gongshi); his younger brothers were Yuanqi 元期, Yuanba, Yuanxiang, Yuanxuan, Yuantai, Yuanheng, Yuanzhi, Yuanding, Yuankai, Yuanzhen, Yuanli, and Yuanzhu. His wife was née Zhang. He placed thirtieth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and thirty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Dazhang, registered in Yin County, Ningbo Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was a county school student specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Zuyao; he ranked thirty-sixth in his family and was aged thirty-one, born on the fifteenth day of the fifth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xun, a Prefectural Registrar; his grandfather’s name and annotated title are illegible (□〔□□〕); his father was Fan. His father’s former wife was née Dong, and his mother was née Chai. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Dashao and Daxia, and his wife was née Wu. He placed seventeenth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and seventy-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Que Jiyu, registered in Nanxi County, Xuzhou Prefecture, Sichuan, belonged to a civilian household and was an Imperial University student specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Shujing; he ranked first in his family and was aged thirty, born on the fourth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Jue, a County Vice Magistrate; his grandfather was Shouwan; his father was Ji; and his mother was née Yang. Both parents were living. His elder brother was Shitai, his younger brother was Shiyu, and his wife was née Shuai. He placed sixty-fourth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and 260th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhong Zhen, registered in Hepu County, Lianzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, belonged to a civilian household and was an annual tribute student specializing in the Classic of Poetry. His courtesy name was Yufu; he ranked first in his family and was aged thirty-one, born on the second day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Mo; his grandfather was Xin; his father was Wen; and his mother was née Li. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yang, Zhuan, Lun, and Jie, and his wife was née Liu. He placed twenty-fifth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and fifty-seventh in the Metropolitan Examination.

title: 嘉靖四十一年進士登科錄
text:
董原道貫四川重慶府巴縣民籍府學生
治詩經字性之行一年三十五三月初八日生
曾祖文昱〔縣丞〕祖溥〔學正〕父誥母母氏繼母張氏
永感下弟明道娶梁氏繼娶楊氏
四川鄉試第四十八名會試第二十九名
沈玄華貫浙江嘉興府秀水縣民籍嘉興縣人縣學生
治書經字瑞伯行十一年二十四十月十三日生
曾祖玟祖璧〔贈知縣〕父銓〔右長史〕嫡母張氏〔封孺人〕生母李氏
慈侍下兄茂之芝華〔監生〕英華茂年堯華〔監生〕茂代華春華稷敷華弟秀華蕣華娶彭氏
浙江鄉試第五十五名會試第一百十五名
===
史櫃貫浙江紹興府會稽縣民籍府學附學生
治詩經字子美行九年二十八十二月十二日生
曾祖吉祖鈿父淮母潘氏
具慶下兄桂〔中書舍人〕朮〔監生〕本弟栻梓機集娶曹氏
浙江鄉試第二十七名會試第一百七十名
林焺貫福建福州府閩縣儒籍國子生
治春秋字貞耀行二年二十三九月初六日生
曾祖元美〔知府贈南京吏部尚書加贈太子太保〕祖瀚〔南京兵部尚書贈太子太保謚文安〕父庭機〔南京禮部右侍郎〕母李氏〔累封淑人〕
具慶下兄炫〔通政司右參議〕烇〔工部主事〕爌〔知府〕爚〔工部員外〕烺焲燫〔翰林院修撰〕熺烰焵熥煠弟烻烒燆娶陳氏

punctuated:
董原道，貫四川重慶府巴縣，民籍，府學生，治詩經，字性之，行一，年三十五，三月初八日生。曾祖文昱〔縣丞〕，祖溥〔學正〕，父誥，母母氏，繼母張氏。永感下，弟明道，娶梁氏，繼娶楊氏。四川鄉試第四十八名，會試第二十九名。

沈玄華，貫浙江嘉興府秀水縣，民籍，嘉興縣人，縣學生，治書經，字瑞伯，行十一，年二十四，十月十三日生。曾祖玟，祖璧〔贈知縣〕，父銓〔右長史〕，嫡母張氏〔封孺人〕，生母李氏。慈侍下，兄茂之、芝華〔監生〕、英華、茂年、堯華〔監生〕、茂、代華、春華、稷、敷華，弟秀華、蕣華，娶彭氏。浙江鄉試第五十五名，會試第一百十五名。

史櫃，貫浙江紹興府會稽縣，民籍，府學附學生，治詩經，字子美，行九，年二十八，十二月十二日生。曾祖吉，祖鈿，父淮，母潘氏。具慶下，兄桂〔中書舍人〕、朮〔監生〕、本，弟栻、梓、機、集，娶曹氏。浙江鄉試第二十七名，會試第一百七十名。

林焺，貫福建福州府閩縣，儒籍，國子生，治春秋，字貞耀，行二，年二十三，九月初六日生。曾祖元美〔知府贈南京吏部尚書加贈太子太保〕，祖瀚〔南京兵部尚書贈太子太保謚文安〕，父庭機〔南京禮部右侍郎〕，母李氏〔累封淑人〕。具慶下，兄炫〔通政司右參議〕、烇〔工部主事〕、爌〔知府〕、爚〔工部員外〕、烺、焲、燫〔翰林院修撰〕、熺、烰、焵、熥、煠，弟烻、烒、燆，娶陳氏。應天府鄉試第一百十五名，會試第一百九十五名。
translation_en:
Dong Yuandao 董原道 was registered in Ba County, Chongqing Prefecture, Sichuan, in the civilian register, and was a prefectural school student. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Xingzhi. He ranked first in family order, was thirty-five years old, and was born on the eighth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Wenyu 〔County Vice Magistrate〕; his grandfather was Pu 〔School Director〕; and his father was Gao. His mother was Lady Mu [?], and his stepmother was Lady Zhang. His parents were deceased. His younger brother was Mingdao. He married Lady Liang and subsequently Lady Yang. He placed forty-eighth in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and twenty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shen Xuanhua 沈玄華 was registered in Xiushui County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, in the civilian register, and was a native of Jiaxing County and a county school student. He specialized in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Ruibo. He ranked eleventh in family order, was twenty-four years old, and was born on the thirteenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Wen; his grandfather was Bi 〔posthumously appointed County Magistrate〕; and his father was Quan 〔Right Chief Administrator〕. His father's principal wife was Lady Zhang 〔granted the title Lady, ruren〕, and his birth mother was Lady Li. His father was deceased, and he attended upon his surviving mother. His elder brothers were Maozhi, Zhihua 〔National University student〕, Yinghua, Maonian, Yaohua 〔National University student〕, Mao, Daihua, Chunhua, Ji, and Fuhua; the division of the names Mao and Daihua is uncertain [?]. His younger brothers were Xiuhua and Shunhua. He married Lady Peng. He placed fifty-fifth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and one hundred fifteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shi Gui 史櫃 was registered in Kuaiji County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, in the civilian register, and was an additional student of the prefectural school. He specialized in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Zimei. He ranked ninth in family order, was twenty-eight years old, and was born on the twelfth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Ji; his grandfather was Dian; his father was Huai; and his mother was Lady Pan. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Gui 桂 〔Secretariat Drafter〕, Shu 朮 〔National University student〕, and Ben; his younger brothers were Shi 栻, Zi, Ji 機, and Ji 集. He married Lady Cao. He placed twenty-seventh in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and one hundred seventieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Lin Sheng 林焺 was registered in Min County, Fuzhou Prefecture, Fujian, in the Confucian scholar register, and was a National University student. He specialized in the Spring and Autumn Annals; his courtesy name was Zhenyao. He ranked second in family order, was twenty-three years old, and was born on the sixth day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Yuanmei 〔Prefect, posthumously appointed Minister of Personnel at Nanjing and additionally Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent〕; his grandfather was Han 〔Minister of War at Nanjing, posthumously appointed Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, with the posthumous name Wen'an〕; his father was Tingji 〔Right Vice Minister of Rites at Nanjing〕; and his mother was Lady Li 〔successively granted honors culminating in the title Lady, shuren〕. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Xuan 炫 〔Right Assistant Commissioner of the Office of Transmission〕, Quan 烇 〔Secretary in the Ministry of Works〕, Kuang 爌 〔Prefect〕, Yue 爚 〔Vice Director in the Ministry of Works〕, Lang 烺, Yi 焲, Lian 燫 〔Senior Compiler in the Hanlin Academy〕, Xi 熺, Fu 烰, Gang 焵, Tong 熥, and Zha 煠. His younger brothers were Yan 烻, Shi 烒, and Qiao 燆. He married Lady Chen. He placed one hundred fifteenth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and one hundred ninety-fifth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wang Tingfu, courtesy name Liangqing, was registered in Fuliang County, Raozhou Prefecture, Jiangxi, in a civilian household. A county school student specializing in the Book of Changes, he ranked twenty-fourth among his male siblings and cousins and was aged thirty-six, born on the sixth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ruzheng; his grandfather, Qingzhong; his father, Wensheng; and his mother, née Hou. Both parents were deceased. His younger brother was Tingxiang, and his wife was née Li. He placed forty-third in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 234th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liu Jingwei, courtesy name Daofu, was registered in Jinxian County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi, in a civilian household, and was a native of Nanchang County. An attached student of the county school specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked ninth among his male siblings and cousins and was aged twenty-nine, born on the fourteenth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yuanjing; his grandfather, Zongzheng; his father, Wu; and his mother, née Jin. His father was living and his mother deceased. His elder brothers were Jinglun, Jingji (Steward), Jingbang, and Jingshi; his younger brother was Jingming. His wife was née Zhou. He placed ninety-second in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and twenty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Shihua, courtesy name Maocheng, was registered in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, in a military household. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked fourteenth among his male siblings and cousins and was aged thirty-five, born on the twentieth day of the fourth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Ling, a holder of a seventh-rank prestige title; his grandfather was Jie, an Assistant Prefect of a department; his father was Dagang, posthumously granted the title of Secretary in the Ministry of Justice; and his mother was née Shao, posthumously granted the title of Lady of Repose. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Shifang (Prefect) and Shiying; his younger brothers were Shimei and Shifan. His wife was née Shao. He placed seventy-fourth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 169th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Su Yu, courtesy name Junming, was registered in Rugao County, Taizhou Department, Yangzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, in a civilian household. A county school student specializing in the Book of Rites, he ranked third among his male siblings and cousins and was aged twenty-eight, born on the twenty-second day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Qi; his grandfather, Lian; his father, Fei (County Registrar); and his mother, née Zhang. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were En and Zhi (an Imperial University student), and his wife was née Sun. He placed fiftieth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 223rd in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Xu Fuyuan 許孚遠, registered in a civilian household in Deqing County, Huzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, was a county school student specializing in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Mengzhong, he ranked first in his family, and he was twenty-eight, born on the second day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Zongming, his grandfather Fu, his father Song, and his mother née Shen; his parents and at least one grandparent were living, his younger brothers were Daoyuan, Zhiyuan, and Xingyuan, and his wife was née Shu; he placed forty-fifth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and thirty-sixth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Xuezeng 陳學曾, registered in a military household of Dongsheng Right Guard and originally from Yangcheng County, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, was a student of the Zunhua County school in Shuntian Prefecture specializing in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Rulu, he ranked sixth in his family, and he was twenty-nine, born on the twenty-first day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was 𤇍 [reading uncertain], an honorary official for longevity; his grandfather Ming was an Assistant Instructor, his father Cong a District Magistrate, and his mother née Feng; his mother alone survived, his elder brothers were Xueshi, Xueli (an annual tribute student), Xueyi, Xueshu, and Xuekong, his younger brother was Xuemeng, and his wife was née Li; he placed fifty-third in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 182nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zeng Fan 曾璠, registered in an official household of Chengtian Guard, Huguang, and originally from Pengze County, Jiujiang Prefecture, Jiangxi, was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Ziyu, he ranked first in his family, and he was fifty-one, born on the fourth day of the second month. His great-grandfather Gong was a Vice Commander, his grandfather Xun a District Magistrate, his father Hui, his mother née Wang, and his stepmother née Lu; his father alone survived, his elder brothers were Zhong (a Battalion Commander) and He, his younger brothers were Bing and Yue, and his wife was née Cong; he placed thirty-fifth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 130th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cao Zideng 曹子登, registered in a military household of Xingzhou Rear Garrison Guard in Zhili and originally from Changzhou County, Suzhou Prefecture, was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Yijian, he ranked second in his family, and he was twenty-six, born on the nineteenth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather Ding was an Imperial Physician, his grandfather Kui a Clerk in the Imperial Medical Office, his father Yinglong held the honorary title of Secretary in the Ministry of Justice, and his mother, née Huang, held the title of Lady of Peace; both parents were living, his elder brothers were Zichao (a Prefect), Liangfu, Zihe, and Zibang, his younger brothers were Zixiao (a Confucian scholar), Zijin, and Zijin, and his wife was née Zhang; he placed twenty-ninth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 121st in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Lü Huo 呂藿, courtesy name Chenqing, was registered in a civilian household in Lingling County, Yongzhou Prefecture, Huguang. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Rites, he ranked sixty-third in his family’s generational order and was aged thirty-three, born on the twenty-eighth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather Zhong was a County Registrar; his grandfather Hong was an Imperial University student. His father was Diaoyang, and his mother was née Deng; both parents were living. His elder brothers were Jie, Zhi, Hui, and Lan, and his younger brothers were Zao and Hua. His wife was née Yang. He placed fifth in the Huguang Provincial Examination and thirtieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cheng Zhongyin 成鐘音, courtesy name Benxie, was registered in a civilian household in Zunhua County, Shuntian Prefecture, and was a native of Yidu County, Qingzhou Prefecture, Shandong. A county school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked third in his family’s generational order and was aged thirty, born on the ninth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Hai; his grandfather Shan received the honorary title of County Magistrate; and his father Ying was a Surveillance Vice Commissioner. His father’s principal wife, née Li, was posthumously granted the title Lady for Service (ruren); his stepmother, also née Li, was granted the same title; and his birth mother was née Wang. His father was deceased, and he attended his living mother. His elder brothers were Zhongqi and Zhongyan, and his younger brothers were Zhongyi, Zhongchan, and Zhongjing. His wife was née Zhang. He placed eightieth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and second in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Younian 陳有年, courtesy name Dengzhi, was registered in a civilian household in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked thirty-seventh in his family’s generational order and was aged thirty-two, born on the ninth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather Meng’ang and grandfather Hou were each posthumously granted the title of Right Vice Censor-in-chief of the Censorate; his father Kezhai held that office. His mother, née Yu, was granted the title Lady of Chastity (shuren). His father was deceased, and he attended his living mother. His elder brothers were Youxun, an Imperial University student, Youji, and Youfu, also an Imperial University student. His wife was née Shao. He placed second in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and eighty-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Yunji 張允濟, courtesy name Aifu, was registered in a civilian household in Gu’an County, Shuntian Prefecture. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked sixth in his family’s generational order and was aged twenty-seven, born on the nineteenth day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xi; his grandfather Zhi was a Prefectural Vice Prefect; and his father Jiayun was a Subprefectural Clerk. His father’s principal wife was née Li, his stepmothers were née Li and née Wang, and his birth mother was née Zhu. His father was deceased, and he attended his living mother. His elder brothers were Yuncheng, Yunsheng, Yunli, Yunxie, and Yunxi, and his younger brothers were Yunji and Yunxiu. His wife was née Jin. He placed fifty-sixth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 236th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Wang Ximing, courtesy name Tianyu, was registered in a civilian household in Xiushui County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, and was a native of Wujiang County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region. A county school student specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged twenty-six, and born on the eighteenth day of the first lunar month. His great-grandfather was Qin, his grandfather Pin, and his father Luan; his mother was née Zhong. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Li and Lin, and his wife was née Qian. He placed fifty-seventh in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and seventy-first in the Metropolitan Examination.

Ma Yize, courtesy name Suiqing, was registered in a civilian household in Changzhou County, Suzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and was a native of Wu County. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-three, and born on the fifth day of the twelfth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Sheng, his grandfather Wenyu, and his father Yin; his mother was née Gu, and his stepmother née Yi. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Yizhou, and his wife was née Zhu. He placed fifteenth in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and twenty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Shi Xu, courtesy name Kemin, was registered in a civilian household in Yongxin County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-five, and born on the second day of the ninth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Wenzhuang, his grandfather Jin, and his father Zhen; his mother was née He. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Xun and Jiang, and his wife was née Wang. He placed forty-eighth in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and fiftieth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Chen Xueyi, courtesy name Erpin, was registered in a civilian household in Nan’an County, Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian. A county school student specializing in the Book of Changes, he was second in birth order, aged thirty-one, and born on the sixteenth day of the tenth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yong, his grandfather Zuo, and his father Duanlang, an Instructor in the School of Medicine; his mother was née Zhuang. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Xuekong, Xuemeng, Xuekui, and Liangyan; his younger brothers were Xuezhu, Xuecheng, and Xuegao. His wife was née Huang. He placed fortieth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and ninety-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

吳焯〔貫廣西柳州府賓州民籍，上林縣人，國子生，治禮記，字純伯，行一，年三十七，十月十七日生〕。曾祖道應，祖能，父邦柱〔教諭〕，母施氏。重慶下，弟煒，娶廖氏。廣西鄉試第五名，會試第一百二十五名。

賈應元〔貫順天府遵化縣軍籍，山西平陽府臨汾縣人，縣學附學生，治易經，字仁甫，行一，年二十七，十一月二十五日生〕。曾祖鳳〔恩例冠帶〕，祖榮，父相，母傅氏。具慶下，弟應文、應魁、應鴻，娶高氏。順天府鄉試第四十七名，會試第一百五十名。
translation_en:
Lin Qiaoxiang, courtesy name Tinghan, was registered in a military household in Jinjiang County, Quanzhou Prefecture, Fujian, and was an attached student of the prefectural school specializing in the Book of Changes (Yijing); second in birth order, he was twenty years old and was born on the tenth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Yu, his grandfather Puqin, and his father Cheng; his father's principal wife was née Zheng and his birth mother née Zhang; his father was deceased and his mother living; his elder brother was Qiaocai and his younger brothers Qiaosen and Qiaozhu; he was betrothed to a woman née Zhang and ranked thirty-ninth in the Fujian Provincial Examination and 187th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Cai Kexian, courtesy name Ziqi, was registered in a civilian household in Cheng'an County, Guangping Prefecture, in the directly administered region, and was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Changes (Yijing); second in birth order, he was twenty-seven years old and was born on the twelfth day of the intercalary twelfth month. His great-grandfather was He, his grandfather Guo, and his father Shaoxian, an annual tribute student; his mother was née Liu and both parents were living; his elder brother Kejiao was a prefectural judge and his younger brother was Kejiu; he married a woman née Wu and ranked sixth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 219th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Zhuo, courtesy name Chunbo, was registered in a civilian household in Bin Subprefecture, Liuzhou Prefecture, Guangxi, was a native of Shanglin County, and was a student of the Imperial University specializing in the Book of Rites (Liji); first in birth order, he was thirty-seven years old and was born on the seventeenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Daoying, his grandfather Neng, and his father Bangzhu, a school instructor; his mother was née Shi, and both his parents and grandparents were living; his younger brother was Wei; he married a woman née Liao and ranked fifth in the Guangxi Provincial Examination and 125th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Jia Yingyuan, courtesy name Renfu, was registered in a military household in Zunhua County, Shuntian Prefecture, was a native of Linfen County, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, and was an attached student of the county school specializing in the Book of Changes (Yijing); first in birth order, he was twenty-seven years old and was born on the twenty-fifth day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Feng, who had been granted the honorary privilege of wearing official cap and girdle under provisions for imperial favor; his grandfather was Rong and his father Xiang; his mother was née Fu and both parents were living; his younger brothers were Yingwen, Yingkui, and Yinghong; he married a woman née Gao and ranked forty-seventh in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 150th in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Hong Xin 洪忻, courtesy name Shouqing, was registered in a military household in Puzhou, Shanxi, and was a native of Dingbian Guard. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents, he was third in birth order, aged thirty-two, and born on the twenty-second day of the second month. His great-grandfather was Jingwen; his grandfather, Xi; and his father, Jiuchou, a Steward of Provisions. His father’s former wife was née Guo, his mother née Feng, and his stepmother also née Feng. His father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brothers were Bu, an official awaiting selection for appointment, and Wei; his younger brother was Yue. He married a woman née Guo and subsequently a woman née Yao. He placed eighth in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 225th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Xuzhi 王續之, courtesy name Daqing, was registered in a civilian household in Nanchong County, Shunqing Prefecture, Sichuan. A prefectural school student specializing in the Book of Changes, he was first in birth order, aged twenty-nine, and born on the twentieth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Rui; his grandfather, Xiwen, was granted the title of Secretary in the Ministry of Revenue; and his father, Ting, was Right Vice Minister of Revenue at Nanjing. His father’s former wife, née Chen, was posthumously granted the title of Lady of Repose; his mother, née Yang, was granted the same title. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Heng, Hong, Xuan, and Chen; his younger brothers were Chuozhi, Jizhi, Suizhi, Jizhi, Buzhi, and Xianzhi. He married a woman née Yong. He placed thirty-first in the Sichuan Provincial Examination and eighty-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Fei Yaonian 費堯年, courtesy name Xizhi, was registered in a civilian household in Yanshan County, Guangxin Prefecture, Jiangxi. A county school student specializing in the Book of Documents, he was third in birth order, aged twenty-five, and born on the eleventh day of the first month. His great-grandfather, Fan, was posthumously granted the titles of Grand Master for Splendid Happiness, Pillar of State, Junior Guardian concurrently serving as Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent, Minister of Revenue, and Grand Secretary of the Hall of Military Glory. His grandfather, Wan, was formerly a Bureau Director in the Ministry of Works; his father, Maowen, was a Magistrate; and his mother was née Zhang. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Henian and Guinian; his younger brother was Changnian. He married a woman née Wei. He placed thirty-second in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and 109th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Guo Fei 郭棐, courtesy name Duzhou, was registered in a military household in Nanhai County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, and was a native of Panyu County. An Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes, he was first in birth order, aged thirty-four, and born on the twentieth day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Yu; his grandfather, Zheng; his father, Dazhi, a Magistrate; and his mother, née Liang. His parents and at least one grandparent were living. His younger brothers were Pan, a tribute scholar, and Li. He married a woman née Zhao and subsequently another woman née Zhao. He placed sixty-third in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and twenty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

游季勳〔貫江西南昌府豐城縣軍籍，國子生，治詩經，字懋甫，行二，年三十二，九月初二日生〕。曾祖弼〔長史〕，祖潛〔知州〕，父本〔聽選官〕，母甘氏。慈侍下，兄孟炎、慶炎、仲炎、叔炎，弟景炎、宗炎、際炎，娶鄧氏。江西鄉試第二十一名，會試第五十八名。
translation_en:
Zhu Cha, courtesy name Ziqian, was registered in a military household in Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang. A supplementary student of the county school, he specialized in the Book of Changes. He ranked eighteenth in family birth order and was thirty-three sui, born on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Xuan, holder of a seventh-rank prestige title; his grandfather was Wenshi, a District Magistrate; his father was Shi, and his mother was née Yu. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Yin and Wan; his younger brothers were Hui, Guan, Ding, Ning, Yi, and Yan. He married a woman née Zhang. He placed forty-first in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 102nd in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wang Feng, courtesy name Lianfu, was registered in a civilian household in Jiashan County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, and was a native of Xiushui County. An added-quota student of the prefectural school, he specialized in the Book of Documents. He ranked first in family birth order and was twenty-nine sui, born on the twenty-first day of the fourth month. His great-grandfather was Xian, his grandfather was Yu, his father was Zhou, and his mother was née Xu. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Hua and Yan. He married a woman née Gu. He placed eighty-first in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 221st in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Dazhong, courtesy name Guozhen, was registered in a civilian household in Xiushui County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, and was a native of Pinghu County. A student of the county school, he specialized in the Book of Documents. He ranked first in family birth order and was twenty-seven sui, born on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Tao; his grandfather was 𤇍 [reading uncertain]; his father was Zaidao, an Imperial University student; and his mother was née Shen. Both parents were living. His elder brothers were Daya, Daqi, Dashou, Dazhang, Dashao, Daxiang, Dafeng, Dayi, Dacheng, Daming, Dalun, Dabin (大賔), Dabin (大賓) [apparent duplication?], Dacheng (大澄), Daxue, and Daben. He married a woman née Yao. He placed eighth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and sixteenth in the Metropolitan Examination.

You Jixun, courtesy name Maofu, was registered in a military household in Fengcheng County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi. An Imperial University student, he specialized in the Book of Odes. He ranked second in family birth order and was thirty-two sui, born on the second day of the ninth month. His great-grandfather was Bi, an Administrator; his grandfather was Qian, a Department Magistrate; his father was Ben, an official awaiting selection for appointment; and his mother was née Gan. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Mengyan, Qingyan, Zhongyan, and Shuyan; his younger brothers were Jingyan, Zongyan, and Jiyan. He married a woman née Deng. He placed twenty-first in the Jiangxi Provincial Examination and fifty-eighth in the Metropolitan Examination.

translation_en:
Zhu Yingshi, registered in a military household of the Yulin Left Guard and originally from Yuyao County, Shaoxing Prefecture, Zhejiang, was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes; his courtesy name was Zizhong, he ranked first in birth order, and he was aged twenty-eight, born on the thirtieth day of the first month. His great-grandfather was Ying; his grandfather, Xiang; his father, Shizeng, a Secretariat Drafter; and his mother, née Chen; both parents were living. His elder brothers were Yingdeng, Yingqi, Yingzhao, and Yingsu, and his younger brothers were Yingdou, Yingshou, and Yingyang; he married a woman née Liang and placed thirty-sixth in the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination and 230th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Sun Yingyuan, registered in an official household of Chengtian Guard, Huguang, was a Chengtian prefectural government student specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Renfu, he ranked first in birth order, and he was aged thirty-two, born on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month. His great-grandfather was Lin, an honorary official recognized for longevity; his grandfather, Da; his father, Jing; his father's former wife, née He; and his mother, née Qin; both parents were living. His younger brothers were Yingheng and Yingshi; he married a woman née Wang and was subsequently betrothed to a woman née Zhang, and he placed fifty-second in the Huguang Provincial Examination and 186th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Yang Nan, registered in a civilian household in Taihe County, Dali Prefecture, Yunnan, was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Documents; his courtesy name was Zhongmu, he ranked first in birth order, and he was aged thirty, born on the fifth day of the third month. His great-grandfather was Xun, posthumously honored as Prefect; his grandfather, Pei, a Prefect; his father, Ruwei; and his mother, née Yang; his father was deceased and his mother living. His younger brother was Ji; he married a woman née Yin and placed eighth in the Yunnan Provincial Examination and 286th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Zhang Jiuge, registered in a military household in Cao Subprefecture, Yanzhou Prefecture, Shandong, was a subprefectural government student specializing in the Book of Odes; his courtesy name was Zhongxuan, he ranked second in birth order, and he was aged thirty-five, born on the twenty-third day of the eleventh month. His great-grandfather was Youxian; his grandfather, Wenju; his father, Tianxu, a Provisioner; his mother, née Du; and his stepmothers, née Chu and née Qiao; his father was deceased and his mother living. His elder brother was Jiude, a tribute scholar (gongshi), and his younger brother was Jiugong; he married a woman née Yang and placed forty-first in the Shandong Provincial Examination and 266th in the Metropolitan Examination.

孫坤〔貫河南歸德府睢州，民籍，州學生，治書經，字順夫，行五，年三十一，六月初四日生〕。曾祖銘〔知縣〕，祖憲文，父守中〔典膳〕，前母朱氏，母劉氏。永感下，兄塘、塏、坦、域〔貢士〕，娶劉氏。河南鄉試第十四名，會試第一百六名。
translation_en:
Chen Jun, registered in Nanhai County, Guangzhou Prefecture, Guangdong, belonged to a military household and was a county school student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Yanwu; his birth order is recorded as “二〇” [?]. He was thirty-five, born on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month. His great-grandfather was Dibao; his grandfather, Qing; his father, He; and his mother, née Yao. Both parents were living. His younger brother was Xun, and he married a woman née Guo. He ranked thirty-fifth in the Guangdong Provincial Examination and 255th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wu Kongxing, registered in Suichang County, Chuzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang, belonged to a civilian household and was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Odes. His courtesy name was Cuiqing, and he was third in birth order, aged thirty, born on the nineteenth day of the tenth month. His great-grandfather was Ting; his grandfather, Su; his father, Wenyuan; and his mother, née Zheng. Both parents were living. His younger brothers were Kai and Ti, and he married a woman née Tong. He ranked eighty-eighth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and 198th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Liang Gang, registered in Jishan County, Jiangzhou, Pingyang Prefecture, Shanxi, belonged to a scholar household and was an Imperial University student specializing in the Book of Changes. His courtesy name was Lifu, and he was third in birth order, aged thirty-six, born on the twenty-first day of the first month. His great-grandfather, Zhu, was a Police Chief; his grandfather, Pu, was an Administrator, posthumously granted the title Grand Master for Governance; his father, Ge, was a Supervising Secretary in the Nanjing Office of Scrutiny for War; and his mother, née Hao, was granted the title Lady. His mother was living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Ji and Zhun, and his younger brothers were Wei and Zhun [the name 埻 appears twice, possibly in error]. He married a woman née Hao and subsequently a woman née Zhang. He ranked first in the Shanxi Provincial Examination and 145th in the Metropolitan Examination.

Sun Kun, registered in Suizhou, Guide Prefecture, Henan, belonged to a civilian household and was a subprefectural school student specializing in the Book of Documents. His courtesy name was Shunfu, and he was fifth in birth order, aged thirty-one, born on the fourth day of the sixth month. His great-grandfather, Ming, was a County Magistrate; his grandfather was Xianwen; and his father, Shouzhong, was a Steward of Provisions. His father's former wife was née Zhu, and his mother was née Liu. Both parents were deceased. His elder brothers were Tang, Kai, Tan, and Yu, the last a tribute scholar (gongshi). He married a woman née Liu. He ranked fourteenth in the Henan Provincial Examination and 106th in the Metropolitan Examination.

萬振孫〔貫直隸廬州府合肥縣，民籍，江西南昌府南昌縣人，府學生，治詩經，字性孺，行一，年三十七，七月十八日生〕。曾祖鉞，祖永權，父瑞〔府通判〕，母羅氏。重慶下。兄庚孫，弟噐孫、似孫、延孫、述孫。娶梁氏。應天府鄉試第一百二十一名，會試第二百九十三名。

叚邦衡〔貫湖廣承天府潛江縣，民籍，縣學生，治詩經，字志伊，行一，年三十九，二月十五日生〕。曾祖憲〔縣主簿〕，祖應奎〔訓導〕，父滋〔教諭〕，母何氏。具慶下。娶何氏。湖廣鄉試第三十七名，會試第二百六十四名。
translation_en:
Yu Nanjin, courtesy name Guoliang, was registered in a civilian household in Pinghu County, Jiaxing Prefecture, Zhejiang. A student of the Directorate of Education specializing in the Book of Documents, he ranked first in family order and was aged forty-four, born on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Zong, his grandfather Cong, and his father Huai, a Salt Office Commissioner. His father's former wife was née Chen, and his mother was née Jiang; his mother was still living and his father deceased. His younger brothers were Nanyang, Nanyong, and Nandu. He married a woman née Song and subsequently a woman née Hu. He placed twenty-eighth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and one hundred fifty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Xu Tingshou, courtesy name Shouzhi, was registered in a civilian household in Chun'an County, Yanzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang. A county school student specializing in the Spring and Autumn Annals, he ranked fifty-fifth in family order and was aged thirty-seven, born on the twenty-sixth day of the eighth lunar month. His great-grandfather was Lun, his grandfather Huan, his father Ye, and his mother née Wang; his mother was still living and his father deceased. His elder brothers were Tingyong and Tingshen. He married a woman née Zhou. He placed tenth in the Zhejiang Provincial Examination and sixty-ninth in the Metropolitan Examination.

Wan Zhensun, courtesy name Xingru, was registered in a civilian household in Hefei County, Luzhou Prefecture, in the directly administered metropolitan region, and was a native of Nanchang County, Nanchang Prefecture, Jiangxi. A prefectural school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked first in family order and was aged thirty-seven, born on the eighteenth day of the seventh lunar month. His great-grandfather was Yue, his grandfather Yongquan, and his father Rui, an Assistant Prefect; his mother was née Luo. His parents and at least one grandparent were still living. His elder brother was Gengsun, and his younger brothers were Qisun, Sisun, Yansun, and Shusun. He married a woman née Liang. He placed one hundred twenty-first in the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination and two hundred ninety-third in the Metropolitan Examination.

Duan Bangheng, courtesy name Zhiyi, was registered in a civilian household in Qianjiang County, Chengtian Prefecture, Huguang. A county school student specializing in the Book of Odes, he ranked first in family order and was aged thirty-nine, born on the fifteenth day of the second lunar month. His great-grandfather was Xian, a County Registrar; his grandfather was Yingkui, an Assistant Instructor; his father was Zi, an Instructor; and his mother was née He. Both parents were still living. He married a woman née He. He placed thirty-seventh in the Huguang Provincial Examination and two hundred sixty-fourth in the Metropolitan Examination.
